speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the terms of Standing Order 43 I ask permission to
move a motion on the grounds of urgent necessity. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard):
That the special committee of the House of Commons on environmental pollution be re-established, composed of not more than 20 members to be later designated by the House, to investigate all matters relating to the discharge of oil by the bulk carrier Irish Stardust into the waters of Johnstone Strait and the Strait of Georgia, including, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, the ownership and operating authority of the ship; the condition of the ship both before and after the incident; the role played before, during and subsequent to the incident by each and every agency established by act of parliament with responsibilities related to preventing or minimizing the damage; and the adequacy or inadequacy of relevant legislation and regulations, with powers to report from time to time its observations, opinions and recommendations thereon;
And that the committee be empowered to send for persons, papers and records; to sit during sittings and adjournments of the House either in Ottawa or British Columbia, and to travel between Ottawa and British Columbia; to print from day to day such papers and evidence as may be ordered by the committee; and to appoint from among its members such subcommittees as it may deem advisable or necessary, and to delegate thereto all or any of its powers except the power to report directly to the House.

subsubtopic: VIET NAM-REPORTED CEASE-FIRE VIOLATIONS- CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN SUPERVISORY COMMISSION-METHOD OF REPORTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while it is regrettable, I do not think it is surprising that after a war that has lasted for a generation there has been a continuation after the hour of the cease-fire. In a number of public statements and in representations made to the various parties I drew attention to the possibility that this might be so, and that the international commission should not be expected to undertake its responsibilities immediately, that it was necessary to provide some time before the cease-fire could be considered to be in effect. However, I do hope that this situation will not continue and that we will then be in a position to carry out our responsibilities in the hope that the truce will in fact be observed.

It is not clear from the reports I have heard whether there are charges in fact that Canadians did give this information or whether in fact these were simply third-hand reports to the effect that somehow some information had got into the hands of the Americans, perhaps through Canadian eyes. Our personnel on the old International Control Commission were authorized to give individual reports only to Ottawa. They were never authorized to give reports to any other country, including the United States, and that is the situation today. I do hope that the measures we are taking will remove even the suggestion that we might be engaged in spying activities.

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been several other members who have spoken before me in this debate on capital punishment, and I should like to congratulate them. They have all spoken eloquently and, I am sure, from deep conviction. This topic so transcends in its value many of the others we have before us that, in my view, it does not admit of partisanship.
I regret that I cannot agree with all those who have spoken before me, including members of my own party, because I cannot agree with those who think it is proper for the state to deprive its citizens of their lives. We have heard much argument in favour of that proposition, Mr. Speaker, and we shall hear more. In fact, I am resigned, as I comprehend the situation now, to being on the losing side of this debate.

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Oh, no.
January 29, 1973

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext: My hon. friends say no, but I am afraid that too many members of this House will not vote according to their consciences, but that they will vote according to the way they believe their constituents want them to vote.

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext: What is wrong with that?

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
That, of course, would result in the reinstatement of the death penalty in this country. I hope I am wrong in that assessment. I hope I am wrong because if there was one thing that impelled me to leave private life and come to this House, if there was one motivating force, it was the belief that the most sacred thing in existence is human life, and the most lasting and beautiful things that men do are those things they do to enhance it.
None of us is here to impose harsher restrictions on life. In my submission, we are here for one thing and one thing only, and that is to ensure that Canada is a good place to be and a country in which everyone may be free to pursue the course he deems best for him. It is only when people behave in such a way that is a menace to the happiness and well-being of their fellow citizens that the state has the right to intervene. Even then, in my submission, that right of intervention is qualified in this way, that there must be as little force as necessary to ensure the public safety. This is the rule followed in the courts of this country when a person is accused of assault and pleads self-defence. The rule is that some force or some restraint may be allowed, but only enough to repel the attack. I believe that approach is the one which the government should take toward crime. If that principle were to apply, then capital punishment would disappear in this country for all time, regardless of circumstance.
Capital punishment does not protect anyone who could not as effectively be protected by imprisonment for life, if necessary, of the murderer, and I shall deal with that later. We will hear many facts and statistics on both sides of this question. We will hear pro and con on the proposition that capital punishment is a deterrent to murder. We will hear, and I wish this were not so, from many people who will claim that obedience to the word of God Himself requires the reinstatement of capital punishment.
I have received, as I am sure all hon. members have, a good deal of mail on this topic. It has come from those on both sides of the question, but the central theme repeated in nearly every piece of pro-hanging mail I have received, the common theme that runs through all of these reten-tionist's letters is this blasphemy on the name of a being whom all of us, regardless of our religious affiliations or backgrounds, have been taught to believe is above all else, a God of love.
I do not propose to tell you how God feels about this. I am not that arrogant. He does not tell me how He feels on this or any other human concern. But I was raised a Christian, and the most puzzling anomaly in the pro-hanging argument is the ability of the proponents of capital punishment to equate the Christ of the manger, the Man-God who chose to come among us as a weakling infant and who suffered Himself to be reviled, tormented and beaten, and finally murdered in a horrible fashion, but who in the midst of all that was able to forgive his tor-menters, with a person of stern being who demands an eye for an eye. I cannot understand that.
Capital Punishment
Let me quote from Hansard on this matter. Almost seven years ago the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) was asked a question about God's will in the matter of capital punishment. He said, as recorded at page 3286 of Hansard for March 28, 1966:
Mr. Speaker, may I say very simply to the hon. member as seriously as he asked the question, that in all the teaching I received about God and about the duties of all men to God the central point was that mercy and charity in the human breast and human mind are the most obvious and most essential characteristics of a religious and godly life. This is as true for society collectively as it is for every individual in society. Second, all the teaching I received on the subject has taught me that it is not right for me to state certain ideas and seek refuge in the assertion that they come from God but that it is much more important for me, as it is for all members in this house, to use the intelligence and the conscience which God gave us to arrive at the conclusion at which we are intended to arrive as human beings exercising our own will.
I share those sentiments of the hon. member for York South. I have not heard them better put and I shall not try to improve upon them. We learned from different teachers, but the principles were the same. We learned, I think that the same principles are common to all human institutions, and if one of them is immutable and universal it must be that human beings, individually and collectively, are the most precious things in the world.
I do not oppose capital punishment because I harbour any sympathy or concern over the fate of murderers. I must confess that I do not spend too much time mulling over their fate. I do care very much about the society in which I live and the effect on that society of state murder. If I may quote a former member of this House, I should like to cite a speech by the former member for Winnipeg South, Mr. Sherman.
He said on March 28, 1966:
I am opposed to the death penalty because it brutalizes me and brutalizes society. It forces me to descend to the same level as the murderer I am hanging. It is sanctioned murder and I resent having to participate in it or have any part in it because it drag me down to the level of the person who is sentenced to death.
That is the matter we should be concerned about, Mr. Speaker. The society that puts people to death is a sick society. It is sick because those societies that insist on the practice almost invariably choose the most painful methods of execution available to them.
There have always existed painless ways to kill people. If those proponents of capital punishment really believe it is necessary as a deterrent to others, or for public safety, they could accomplish their aim in painless fashion. But they do not, Mr. Speaker. They strangle their prisoner; they break his neck; they crush his windpipe. They send thousands of volts of electricity through his body and cook his insides. They choke him to death with poison gas. Did you ever hear of a society that killed its prisoners by giving them an overdose of a pleasant, easeful narcotic? That would be very simple. But if I were to propose in this chamber the adoption of that course, the angry reaction from one end of the country to the other would be heard by all hon. members. The reason such a reaction is that a prisoner would not be struggling in agony, in pain, even as he surrendered up his most precious possession, his life.

January 29, 1973
Capital Punishment
In my experience these proponents of hanging are the same people who are the first to moan piously about the fate of the fetus whenever the question of abortion is raised. Even before a fetus has achieved growth to the point where it could survive in the human environment by itself, they insist that its quasi-human status be prolonged. Why? Is it because of their reverence for human life? Or is it because they insist that the errant woman who carries that fetus should suffer the shame, the indignity, the torment, and the opprobrium of society for her so-called crime? I wonder, but I don't wonder very long.
There is one reason, and one reason alone why people insist on capital punishment, and that is revenge. It is easy to understand why people seek revenge. It is easy to sympathize with them. I have three small children, Mr. Speaker. If one of those children were harmed or killed by someone, my immediate reaction would be to want to murder in return, as horribly as I could contrive to do it, the person responsible. That wish is not rational, and its fulfilment would do me a terrible disservice. It demeans me and brings me to the level of that pitiable creature who wronged my child. It renders me no less contemptible than the murderer. I submit that to the extent that one of us is demeaned and sickened in this fashion, society is contaminated by the disease. I do not want that kind of society, and I do not want it for my children.
It has been said by those who want to reinstate hanging in this country that violent crime is rising everywhere and that people are not safe on the streets. I do not know whether this is true. Certainly, I have never encountered any difficulty walking the streets of this or any other Canadian city in which I have lived or visited. But supposing it were true, would the reinstatement of capital punishment change it very much? I seriously doubt that. I believe that our society places far too high a premium on material things, and far too low a premium on human well-being and safety. For that reason, I urge a much more drastic approach to crimes of violence, crimes against the person as opposed to crimes against property.
Only last week I read about a man who kidnapped three young people, two girls and a boy. He struck the young man over the head with an axe, then raped the two girls, struck them over the heads with his axe, and threw all three of his victim into a river. He was convicted of these offences and received a sentence of 18 years in prison. In my opinion, that is not enough. I believe he should never again see daylight except in the exercise yard of some prison, not to punish him but to protect society against the possibility that he would do it again, and to protect him from himself because he has shown that he cannot cope with life among us. His violence could be directed anywhere, even against himself. I do not believe that a man who viciously and wantonly attacks like that is a misunderstood individual. I understand him; I understand him all to well. I understand the message he is sending. He is saying he cannot live in our society, that he cannot cope with our society, and that for his own good and that of society he should be locked up. That goes not only for those who kill people, who kill others, but it also goes for all violent people.
But it is not necessary for us to authorize the state to do something that we have not the courage to do ourselves.

The killing of another human being guarantees only one thing. If he is a murderer, it guarantees he will not be here tomorrow to repeat his offence. However, that is equally true of car thieves, forgers and pickpockets, and it is not the answer. We must learn to distinguish between the crime and the person. Just as there are non-capital crimes committed by people who would never be turned loose, who ought to be imprisoned for life, there are capital crimes committed by people for whom one day in jail would be unnecessary. This kind of approach and emphasis on public safety and rehabilitation, with the one before the other, would take a great deal of money to put into effect. The present slapdash approach to sentencing and parole, which is under justified attack from all sides, would have to be scrapped. In its place we should put a system which does not punish but protects, which does not destroy but renews where possible. It is always more difficult to save a bad situation than to quit cold and move along; but very often, Mr. Speaker, the rewards are worth the trouble.
We are told that capital punishment is a deterrent. If that were so it would seem to me that when it was suspended for all but one category of murders, the number of offences within that one category would either stabilize immediately or diminish. Yet we find, and these are the only statistics I shall cite, that in 1968, the first year after the Criminal Code was amended, there were eight persons charged with the murder of policemen, the only offence which still carried the death penalty. That was an increase of 800 per cent over the previous year when only one person was so charged. In 1969, that figure fell to seven persons charged with murdering a policeman, and in 1970 it fell back to one. If those figures tell us anything, it is that the presence of the death penalty did not deter anyone, and that the incidence of crime, violent and otherwise, is a totally unpredictable thing.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe, and I am getting rather weary of the proposition, that the burden of proof in this matter rests upon me or upon those who support my position. In a sense our position is analagous to that of defence counsel, and I submit that the only thing incumbent upon us is to demonstrate a reasonable doubt. The burden of proof, if any proof exists, is clearly upon those who would commit this state perpetually to a policy of cold blooded murder. They have not established even a prima facie case for their position, Mr. Speaker, and their only contributions have been those of obfuscation, bloated rhetoric and alarmist nonsense about what happens on the streets when the sun goes down. They have deliberately tried to confuse the issue of rising violence in general with that of whether the state should demand and collect a life for a life, and they are behaving irresponsibly when they do so.
I do not believe you can prove ultimate principles, Mr. Speaker. You cannot demand a reason for everything. But that does not mean that these principles are unintelligible or imponderable or that they cannot be reflected upon. And surely one of them is that no man, individually or through the agency of the state, has the moral right to kill another, unless his own life is in peril. I want to deal now with the question of our responsibility as Members of
January 29, 1973

Parliament. The theory is being advanced, most recently by the Canadian Association of Police Chiefs, that members ought not to vote according to their individual beliefs or their consciences but according to what has been described as the expressed will of the Canadian people. I do not know of any satisfactory way in which to determine the wish of the electorate, short of holding a plebiscite and requiring every citizen to take part in it upon pain of penalty. But even if there were a way to determine the wish of the electorate it would make no difference to me. I intend to vote according to my conscience, because I believe this is my responsibility as a Member of Parliament.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
In support of that position I should like to quote part of an essay on representative government by John Stuart Mill. He says that he disagrees with those who insist that a Member of Parliament is in fact an instructed delegate. He goes on to say that constituents:
... are entitled to a full knowledge of the political opinions and sentiments of the candidate; and not only entitled, but often bound, to reject one who differs from themselves on the few articles which are the foundation of their political belief: That in proportion to the opinion they entertain of the mental superiority of a candidate, they ought to put up with his expressing and acting on opinions different from theirs on any number of things not included in their fundamental articles of belief: That they ought to be unremitting in their search for a representative of such calibre as to be entrusted with full power of obeying the dictates of his own judgment: That they should consider it a duty which they owe to their fellow-countrymen, to do their utmost toward placing men of this quality in the legislature: and that it is of much greater importance to themselves to be represented by such a man than by one who professes agreement in a greater number of their opinions: for the benefits of his ability are certain, while the hypothesis of his being wrong and their being right on the points of difference is a very doubtful one.
I hope that members will listen to that message, Mr. Speaker, and that those who have not been listening will read it because I think it is an important doctrine. I hope they will be able to vote according to their own consciences, and when they have finished voting I hope they will be able to contemplate their action free of doubt. It is a fearful responsibility and I am sure most Members of Parliament wish, as I do, that they did not have to accept it.
For me, once I have been forced to take the responsibility, the choice is relatively simple. I have been able to make it a highly personal issue. Recently my wife and I were fortunate enough to have born to us a son. He is now two months old, a little tiny person just becoming aware of the world around him. Some of the happiest moments that I spend-and they are very few these days-are with this little person before I come up here to work in the morning. He is not capable of doing any wrong now but in the years to come if I fail him as a father-and God knows I am a fallible man-or if something vital to humanity is left out of his make-up, he could go wrong. He could come to grievous harm or even do harm to others. I do not like to think that will ever happen, but I have to recognize that it could. Then, I have to ask myself if I could ever contemplate with calm and equanimity the idea that one day my son could be taken out and brutally strangled because he failed or I failed? Could I ever bring myself to believe that
Capital Punishment
society was in some way better off because it destroyed that body that I helped to create? Could I ever believe that one decent purpose was served by choking off for all time that brightness and being of my son? Mr. Speaker, the answer is, whatever he has done, God help me, no, I cannot. I will not ever believe that. My son is no different from anyone else's son.
Those are my arguments, Mr. Speaker. They may not be strong enough to move any hearts. They are not buttressed by ledgers full of facts; they are intuitive. But they are none the less valid because I believe that when men and women presume to decide whether they should kill their brothers and sisters there are more important things to consider than facts. I think they should listen to their inner voice. I have listened to mine and it tells me simply that killing is wrong and we should not do it. I urge all members to support the government bill.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it pleases me that I rise immediately after the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly) to make my remarks on this very difficult bill before us. He and I come from similar professional backgrounds and share, from our experience of the world as journalists, the belief that the death penalty is wrong.
My stand as an abolitionist goes back about 11 years to December 11, 1962. In Toronto, at the Don jail on a very cold drizzly night when Canadian society for the last time-and I hope it was for the last time-took life in the name of its laws. That was the occasion of the hanging of Ronald Turpin and Arthur Lucas, both convicted of capital murder. To me, as a young newsman of 22 or 23 years, it seemed like something out of "A Tale of Two Cities", something very medieval or Dickensian; waiting until midnight after all the lights had gone out in the jail and that single, symbolic light remained; waiting for the 30 or 35 minutes for the crowd of drunks to emerge from the nearby bars and the motocycle gangs to come revving their engines; waiting till that light went out and the notice was posted on the door of the jail. Then, I went with the other newsmen to the old city hall where I listened to the sheriff of York county, a witness to the hanging, a man shaking and shaken, declare that he would never again have any part of it, that he had changed his views on the necessity for the death penalty.
In the dark of night, in the 1960's, in Canada, two men were hanged, back to back, because society said that would stop somebody else from committing the same crime. I cannot believe that, Mr. Speaker. I do not believe that any member of this House, having considered the mass of material that is being circulated to us, can possibly believe that the death penalty is a deterrent.
We all agree that statistics can be manoeuvred and manipulated to make our point. However, I should like to present a few statistics to show that they do not prove a thing, that they are not conclusive and we must refer to facts, because only then do we find some satisfaction in our views or the possibility of changing our views.
I have a list of the murder rate in various American states, those with the death penalty and those without. I am going to refer to it very briefly. In the State of Alaba-

January 29, 1973
Capital Punishment
ma they have electrocution. According to the latest statistics available for 1971, the murder rate in Alabama was 11.7 per one hundred thousand of population. If I wanted to play with statistics I could go to Rhode Island, which has not had the death penalty for many years. There the murder rate is 2.2 per one hundred thousand. If I were to be more responsible in reciting these statistics I ought to mention those for Massachusetts and Maine. Those states are in about the same part of the U.S.A., both are composed of the same types of people who live in similar environments. In Massachusetts, where electrocution is retained, the murder rate is 2.8; in Maine it is 0.4; so, we still come out ahead in that circumstance. Now let me compare New York with New Jersey. New York, without the penalty, has a rate of 5.4, but New Jersey, with electrocution, has one of 3.9. There, the tendency is in the other direction. What does this prove? It proves nothing when you try to compare murder rates with the imposition of capital punishment or the non-imposition of capital punishment. There is simply no relationship between the punishment and the murder rate.
Of more immediate concern to this House are Canadian statistics. I believe those most recently available are for 1970. The statistics are reported by the various police departments across Canada. I will use them, but I point out the inadequacy of statistics and their use unless there is a very deep study of how those figures are arrived at, and unless they are fully understood and related to the various tables. Briefly, the number of murders reported in Canada in 1970-and this figure will be repeated time and again so I ask hon. members to bear it in mind-was 430. This figure, I repeat, relates to two years ago. According to police records, 430 people were killed. Well, the number of people sent to trial, in other words the number of murder cases that were heard, and I mention murder cases because we are talking about the crime of murder, was 153. Out of 153 cases, only one accused was convicted in 1970 of capital murder under the law of that time; only 34 of 153 were convicted of non-capital murder and 56 were convicted of manslaughter.
So, if we are talking about capital punishment versus non-capital punishment, let us remember that out of 430 cases, or reported cases, there was only one conviction for capital murder. There was a grand total of one convicted out of all that number, under the law. Yet that law remains on the statute books. It is the law of our country and of our society. In other words, we feel that we must take a life, as a society, in order to stop people from taking a life. That is a very strange rationale. Let me repeat the 1970 figure, because we shall return to it again and again. Out of 430 cases or incidents reported by the police departments, one accused was convicted of capital murder. To be fair, there are 33 cases still pending. Nevertheless, one was convicted of capital murder and 153 cases out of 430 incidents went to trial.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) said, in opening this debate the other day, that there is a two-year delay in the provision of adequate statistics and that therefore he would like to have this legislation in existence for another five-year trial period. He suggested that if statistics are to be valid they must be taken from a broad cross-section of

the population; only in that way can you reach any conclusion. Any single set of statistics is of questionable value. I am not sure that we need more statistics.
However, if the minister thinks we do then, since he is a member of the government I support, I am prepared to support him in that position only if we cannot do better. I am sure we all harbour our own doubts as to the proper way statistics should be used, because statistics have been compiled for decades around the world. We have seen exact statistics compiled in the United States over the last ten years. There are our own statistics, as I mentioned a moment ago, for 1970. Indeed, if we need more, let us have more, but what will they show? We have already seen that there was one conviction out of 430 incidents.
The issue of a national referendum was introduced into this debate. I think the Solicitor General referred to it and dealt with the matter much more adequately than I could deal with it. Some question arose about the referendum in California where public opinion demanded the return of the death penalty. That referendum had the force of law; it would not have the force of law in Canada. Much more important and more to the point, it seems to me that if we in this House react to popular issues with popular decisions, there is no reason for the existence of this House. We cannot escape the obligation of making decisions on behalf of those who voted for us. I think we should set a very dangerous precedent indeed if we were to try to escape making such a difficult decision as this through the mechanism of a referendum, and thereby set a precedent that could have an effect in law. In any crisis in future when any unpopular decision would have to be taken by parliament, that is the precedent we would follow.
It is said that the polls show that an overwhelming number of people want the return of the death penalty. Without trying to be biased, and forgive me if I am, I remind hon. members that our system of law and parliamentary procedure is very much based on the British system. I do not think that parliament across the water is disintegrating and I do not think its effectiveness as one of the best trial by chance, true democratic means of carrying on government and holding together a society is failing. I think we respect it and do not try to impute motives to whatever government is at the helm at the moment. It should be remembered that just before the government of Great Britain voted for the permanent abolition of the death penalty, 80 per cent of the people polled had said, "No, we want the death penalty." Would anyone say that the British parliament turned against its people, or that it had not tried to act wisely and carry out its heavy responsibilities under that system.
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) mentioned the RCMP when he spoke in this debate a few days ago. He said that there was great concern over declining morale of the NDP-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to speak about improving the morale of that party, if it needs improving. I was talking about the RCMP. The hon. member for Yukon said that the RCMP suffered from low morale and that morale should not be further eroded as it would be if we permitted the bill before the House to pass. I for one, along with any really involved Canadian who cares for his country and participates in its activities, take great pride in the RCMP and the respect it has brought us around the world. Yet, surely to goodness there is a basic difference to be remembered; they are law-enforcers and we are law-makers. We must take into account their views and their experiences, but the decision is ours. If the morale of the force is low, surely to goodness it is not low because we are not hanging people-even if the RCMP thinks we ought to. We must consider that morale and correct it, if anything is wrong, without resorting to that kind of red herring and without embellishing the kind of argument that pits the morale of that force against society taking human life under its laws.
An old friend of mine who is a prison psychiatrist has written me a letter. He is not a wild-eyed dreamer, but a practical man. He wrote to me and I wrote to him; we do not agree completely, as one can see from the contents of his letter. However, we do not think the issue of the death penalty is simple. It is much more complicated than, "Execute and be safer or do not execute and be unsafe." He wrote:
I would rather confine my remarks to my observations, after ten years of forensic work, on convicted murderers. At least one I know is probably completely innocent. Several others were undoubtedly mentally ill at the time of their offense, but not so markedly so as to convince a court of their lack of guilt by reason of insanity. Several (especially the women) were with a person who committed a murder, but struck no blow themselves, and often deny any knowledge that a murder was planned. Most Canadian killers commit murder only once within a highly-charged emotional relationship, often within the family. It seems entirely capricious to me that some of the accused in a homicide offense are found not guilty for reasons of accident, self-defense, automatism, or are found guilty of manslaughter rather than murder. This might depend on the calibre of the lawyers, the judge, the public reaction to the apparent facts, the demeanour or social class of the accused, etc. The point seems to revolve around this-there is a tradition that the lawbreaker should be punished, and most severely for severe crimes. After society has exacted its retribution, and reminded the populace of its basic sanctions, then how many of these people remain dangerous?
According to the experts, not many remain dangerous. Some do, and we ought to enact laws that will protect us from those few. That does not mean that we need to kill those people in order to be protected. I shall deal with that argument in a moment. What is the relationship between a death penalty and the number of convicted murderers? I read from the second paragraph of this letter:
You tell me that those who wish to retain capital punishment are concerned about the rising crime rate, violence in the streets, and the safety of the public. So are all decent citizens. The growth of crime may have its roots in a very complex causality-e g. the decline of the stable family structure, over-population, urbanization, the dishonesty of corporations or unions, parole, drugs, gov-
Capital Punishment
ernment waste, the Bail Reform Act, the welfare philosophy, the decline of the churches, etc.
Any one of those reasons is important. Not just because the law says you may hang or you may not hang.
I want to make one further quote if I may. This is a quotation from Lewis Lawes who was the warden of Sing Sing Prison for many years. Warden Lawes said:
Not only does capital punishment fail in its justification, but no punishment could be invented with so many inherent defects. It is an unequal punishment in the way it is applied to the rich and to the poor. The defendant of wealth and position never goes to the electric chair or to the gallows. Juries do not intentionally favour the rich, the law is theoretically impartial, but the defendant with ample means is able to have his case presented with every favourable aspect, while the poor defendant often has a lawyer assigned by the court... with no experience.
In making his case the other day, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Yukon showed his great debating skills. These are, I am sure, known not only to members in this House but elsewhere as well. Before I came here I had heard about them. He has what I would call an excessive ability to manoeuvre words and situations. As an example, he quoted the Toronto Star of January 18, 1973, and he seemed to imply, in his use of that quotation, that the rule of majority must be the rule this debate should follow. The hon. member for the Yukon said that in an earlier debate on this subject he had made a long and objective study and had taken a particularly unemotional look at the question. He went on to say that statistics did not prove anything. On that point I must agree.
The Star article the hon. member quoted was cited without reference to its author. The newspaper itself, I would like to make clear, is on record as being in favour of abolition, but it is in favour of abolition with a proviso that would guarantee the real safety of society. I quote from an editorial which appeared in the same newspaper, the Toronto Star, two days later than the article quoted by the hon. member for Yukon. It is headed, "A substitute for the gallows", and reads as follows:
One of the basic problems in the debate over retaining the ban on capital punishment is what to do with hard-core murderers- the type who were almost always hanged under the old system. The penalty for non-capital murder is now, nominally, life imprisonment, but under present practice prisoners sentenced to life may be released on parole after serving 10 years.
If the National Parole Board had an infallible record in selecting prisoners suitable for release, there might be no quarrel with this; but the board is unfortunately anything but infallible. As a result a great many people are haunted by the fear of hardened, vicious killers being turned loose to kill again, and their fears have contributed to the demand for the return of the gallows.
The article goes on, Mr. Speaker:
To meet this problem, Solicitor-General Warren Allmand has indicated that he is considering a mandatory minimum sentence of 25 years for all convicted murderers.
This is altogether too sweeping. Murderers after all, fall into many categories.
The article goes on to make reference to crimes of passion and so on. The article later goes on to say:
But there are other types of murderers for whom long minimum sentences are certainly justified. They include hired killers, political assassins and terrorists, sexual psychopaths and other psychopathic killers. These are the types who, if released, are likely to repeat their crimes. Keeping them under lock and key for as long as possible is therefore a measure of public safety.

January 29, 1973
Capital Punishment
If Allmand's proposed 25-year minimum sentence were restricted to murderers in these classifications, it would do a good deal to reassure the public, and it might disarm a good deal of the opposition to the permanent abolition of the death penalty.
I apologize to the minister if the 25-year minimum idea has been hung upon him but the non. member for St. Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) and I do propose it. I will get back to that point in a moment. I am sure most hon. members are aware that we had intended to propose something along that line. We are not making a formal amendment at this time. We are still considering how the principle might be adjusted a little.
The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly) made reference to the question of crime in the streets. I was pleased to hear that he feels safe in our streets and I must admit that I share his feeling. However, many women and children do not feel safe. In the suburban part of Metropolitan Toronto from which I come there has been a great deal of crime, including several murders, over the last year or two. There has been an increase in drug problems, and evidence of increasing fear among the people. It is unfortunate that people have focussed upon the death penalty as a means of regaining their safety, as if this vengeance would put fear into criminals. I do not believe that retention of the death penalty will have the effect they desire. The general rate of crime has gone up more rapidly than has the murder rate. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot relate the two. I cannot believe that a couple of hangings, terrible as it would be for society to return to that condition, would change the trend of crime.
I agree we have to review the bail system, the parole system and tighten them where necessary. We have to work toward a healthier society, and I appreciate that this sounds lofty, as does being in favour of motherhood and so on. Right now, in my opinion, it is more necessary to work toward this healthier society than it has ever been. Perhaps we should direct ourselves to improving our environment and education-and when I say "education" I mean not just education to be scholarly, but education in coping with the tremendous drives and strains of our day.
While I will, if I must, support the bill before us, I do hope that at a more appropriate time, perhaps in committee, I may argue with its principle to some small degree. I wish to say lhat I would rather not have half the principle, but the whole principle, while recognizing the need for deterrent power and especially the feeling of public safety through whatever final legislation is approved by this House. For that reason, as many are probably aware from statements outside the House, the hon. member for St. Denis and myself will attempt at a more appropriate moment to get a life imprisonment term for first degree murder which will mean a 25-year incarceration period, without release for any reason other than, perhaps, to attend a funeral of a mother whilst under guard escort; 25-years of incarceration with just a possibility of parole to give a glimmer of hope. At this point, I think it is important to put emphasis on the safety of people rather than on that of the criminal.
If some are alarmed at this idea on the grounds of the impossibility of rehabilitation, let them argue the point as statistics become available. Maybe, if they prove their point, this regulation can be rolled back. But only by

parliament. I believe that the taking of life by society has proved not only ineffective, but that it is wrong. Meanwhile I do believe we must give our people some reassurance that we are acting in the interests of their safety.
There are two letters I would like to read, if I may, Mr. Speaker, because I hope that some hon. members have received similar reactions. The first letter reads:
Dear Mr. Fleming:
I have just read in this morning's Gazette that you and Mr. Marcel Prud'homme propose to introduce an amendment to the bill regarding capital punishment whereby convicted murderers would not be eligible for parole for 25 years. Congratulations. I hope you are successful. I have just written my own M. P., Mr. Warren Allmand, to this effect.
Until now, people like myself, and I believe we run into thousands and possibly millions, have had no alternative but to ask for the return of the death penalty because any other punishment was ridiculously easy on the murderer. Loss of freedom for 8-10 years seems ridiculous to me for such a crime anyway, and I believe if you are successful with your amendment the feeling of the population toward banning the death penalty either permanently or temporarily would be completely different.
Mr. Speaker, my time is running short but in conclusion I should like to make reference to the formation in 1964 of the Canadian Society for the Abolition of the Death Penalty. From time to time during this debate we have heard references made to the "do-gooders" who are in favour of motherhood and against sin. Let me give you an idea of what this Society is. First off, it is not a social service agency, though the work that they do is just great and should always be respected. So often the public's view of such organizations is slanted in that sense. It.was founded by a young man named Ted Matlow, who was a law student at the University of Toronto. He had read some news stories and reports and became concerned when this issue was building here that no one in society was trying to focus on the wrongness of taking life under our law. He wrote letters to 30 Members of Parliament and former members of parliament who got together and formed this society.
To show that this is not a matter of political philosophy but rather a matter of conscience and understanding, let me give the House an example of the kind of people who belong to this society. For example, the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) was a member of the founding group. The leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), was also a member of that group. Senator Wallace McCutcheon, who can hardly be described as a left-wing Liberal, was a member of that group. The late Mr. Ross Thatcher was also a member. So was Frank McGee, once a member of this House. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), very respected by his fellow members, especially those on the benches opposite, was a member of that group. All of these were men and women who felt concerned enough to get together and decide to fight for the principle that society should not take life.
I want to make one thing clear as I conclude. This does not for one moment mean that I, as an abolitionist, have any right to be pious, to look down my nose at those people who honestly believe that the death penalty is necessary. If those people succeed in this debate and we
January 29, 1973

return to the law as it stands today, and as it stood before the trial period, then the onus on them will be much greater than that which the rest of us, as abolitionists, will bear if we succeed. Because by voting for retention they in fact carry the weight of society's decision to take a life. If these 120 votes or so succeed, that will start the gallows working again. I do not scoff at the responsibility that they bear or how deep their conviction is within their conscience, for they must live with that. But I am sure that they must be as aware on their side as we are on ours of the real concern. I am not afraid to live with an angry public because of a superficial understanding of what I believe. The retentionists may have the public with them this time, but they must live with themselves if we in fact go back to hanging.
In studying this matter in the past I remember making some reference to what was said by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). It is a small point and not the most important point in this debate. I think the most important point is the issue of deterrence and whether or not society should take life; whether it is for the public good to do so. Public safety is also important. The right hon. member for Prince Albert is on our record as having said that in his own experience as a criminal lawyer he saw one client of his condemned, executed, and then six months later the star Crown witness came foward and confessed to the crime.
I should like to refer to one final letter, if I may. This letter came to me a week or so ago and reads as follows: Dear Mr. Fleming:
I would like to sincerely approve of the proposal to be put forth to the Federal Government (and also by Marcel Prud'homme) re capital punishment.
I cannot quite bring myself to advocate the death penalty for murderers, either of the police doing their duty, or of a civilian, in spite of the fact that my husband and two business associates were murdered in Hamilton in 1937.
The murderer, father of a lawyer in that city, served a term in Kingston, during which time he apparently became a model prisoner and went about teaching religion to other inmates.
He was released some years later-where he is or what he is doing I have no idea, nor do I wish to know, and I never discuss it with anyone.
I did, however, call our member, Mr. Terry O'Connor of Oakville, and told him of this tragedy in my life and of my approval of your proposal-with accent on 25 year minimum sentences.
The guilty man (or woman) has to live with this dreadful act he has committed and perhaps, by the grace of God, can make something of his life.
I support the government, and I hope very much that this bill, after receiving the support of this House on second reading, will go to committee. At that time I hope with my colleague, the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), to make some proposals with regard to a 25 year minimum life sentence and also with regard to the categories of first degree murder.
More than anything, however, I hope that the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly) is wrong-I know that he speaks in honesty and conscience-when he says he believes that the retentionist side will win. I appreciate that all of us have to act in accordance with our own conscience and in light of our own experience, reflecting, of course, the views of our electorate. But I would find it incredible if today we voted for retention, in view of the
Capital Punishment
number of states that have abolished the death penalty and the example of Great Britain, whose government stood in the face of a public that was not fully aware of the situation and voted according to conscience to abolish the death penalty. The British parliament continues its tradition of making difficult as well as easy decisions. Then, there is the example of the United States which has to cope with the terrible dilemma posed by the referendum that was held in California recently and which resulted in a mix-up of the law. I hope that when the moment comes for the final vote, we shall take the responsibility upon ourselves, and as individuals, be we retentionists or abolitionists, vote according to our own mind, not simply reflecting the will of our constituents or any other group.
