speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the calibre of my remarks will be equal to the calibre of the debate we have had to date. I listened with great interest to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), to the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), to the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly), the hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming), and also to the brief remarks, in view of the shortness of time, of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). I think the debate has been of very high calibre.
Let me come down to the nub of the matter. I think parliament wants to know where I stand on the abolition bill. I am going to oppose the bill. I will support only law that retains some from of capital punishment-and I emphasize some form of capital punishment-for planned, premeditated, deliberate killing, known as culpable homicide, and for the killing of a person by violent means where any reasonable person would or ought to know that death would ensue. This is defined as capital murder. That is the provision in the law today, unless this bill receives a vote of confidence in this House.
I support the formula that was devised by the Diefenbaker government under which murder was defined as culpable homicide, categorized either as capital or as noncapital murder. From my experience, only in exceptional cases does a trial judge let the matter go to the jury as capital murder under the formula of 1961. In other words, only when the evidence indicates a certainty that the killing of another person was planned, premeditated, deliberate or caused by violence that was planned and premeditated, and as a result death ensued, is the jury asked to decide, first, whether the murder was capital or non-capital. Ninety-five per cent of cases under the old formula went to the jury as non-capital murder cases, which called for a penalty of life imprisonment. Hence, for most murders the death penalty was abolished as early as 1961. That was the first step in the reform of our criminal law. I think all of us would agree, whether we are abolitionists or retentionists, that that was the case.
Before discussing the merits of my argument for capital punishment as an effective punishment for capital murder, let me repeat that in my opinion-I say this quite frankly-there was no need at this time, when Canada is suffering from a lack of economic policy, to have a debate on this bill.
Why do I say that? Since the Trudeau government was elected in 1968 capital punishment has been abolished as a

January 29, 1973
Capital Punishment
fact, or as we lawyers say, de facto, if not totally by law, or de jure. As the Solicitor General told me last Friday in response to my questions, no one has paid the price according to law by suffering death for killing a police officer or a guard, and no one is waiting in custody for a commutation of the death penalty at this time. Those are the facts and that is where we start on this debate. There has been a complete softening and easing, in my opinion, on capital punishment under the present government with reference to those found guilty of murder and violent crime.
The 1967 bill was only approved by this House of Commons on the grounds that capital punishment would remain for all those convicted of killing police officers and guards. The government would never have been able to get this bill approved by certain areas of this country if that solemn undertaking had not been given by the government, which is lead by the same man today. No sooner had the bill passed than a group of prisoners awaiting penalties had their sentences commuted. There were 12 of them who were found guilty of murdering police officers and guards who had their sentences commuted, and I will deal with their names later. A number of them were awaiting the sentence, but the bill was no sooner passed and received Royal approval than their sentences were commuted. In my opinion, this was a fraud perpetrated on parliament.
The Trudeau government has not changed and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has not changed. All those people convicted of capital murder under this bill will have their sentences commuted as has been done previously. I would rather see a government come in today and say honestly that it intends to abolish capital punishment absolutely, and then let us have a vote on that. Truly that is what we will be voting on when this bill comes back from the committee for third reading.
In my opinion this debate was called by the government for the purpose of sweeping under the carpet serious problems of unemployment and inflation, as well as the suffering and frustration of our senior citizens and those on fixed incomes who are waiting for relief in respect of all these economic cares. In a sense, the Prime Minister has carried out the emasculation of the democratic process by ignoring the will of the people who are asking for immediate relief, and this course is being supported unfortunately by the NDP because it must do so for its own survival. It is that support which is the reason this government, defunct and bankrupt of ideas, is now still in office.
Let me now turn to the names of those people convicted by due process of law in Canada, which means a trial by jury in most provinces, with the exception of one, the right to an appeal and the right with leave, and under certain circumstances without leave, to go to the Supreme Court of Canada, of murdering police officers and guards but who have had their sentences commuted since January 4, 1968. There are 12 in all, and they are as follows: Douglas J. Booth, Rene G. Castellani, Jean-Jacques Boivin, David A. DeLeon, Henri Boivin, Herbert M. Myers, Harold A. Ortt, Ovila Bonlet, Leonard Otto Borg.

By the way, Borg's sentence was commuted on July 3, 1969.
Then we have Clifford Wickett Lurvey, December 23, 1970; William R. Rosik, February 4, 1971, and the twelfth, Thomas Mason Shand, March 8, 1972. So twelve people convicted of murdering police officers and guards had their sentences commuted, even though there was a solemn understanding that if we passed the bill those people convicted of such crimes would be subject to capital punishment. It is true that there is the Royal prerogative, but it was never intended to be used in that fashion. Where a discretion is exercised 100 per cent one way, there is no discretion at all.
The Solicitor General left the impression by his speech, perhaps unintentionally, that there were only four convicted killers of police officers and guards who had their sentences commuted since January 4, 1968, whereas there were four under the 1967 bill but 12 in total since January 4, 1968. I repeat that there were four as a result of the 1967 act, but the government stayed eight executions of killers of police officers and guards while the 1967 bill was being approved and receiving Royal Assent. In brief, all 12 were convicted under the same kind of law. There was no change in 1967 from what existed in 1966, when it comes to that, because in 1967 the law in respect of killing police officers and guards did not change the penalty.
Then on Friday, and I am not breaking a confidence here because this is a matter of information, I received the following letter from the Solicitor General:
Eldon.
I just got more information on your question. There were 17 commutations on January 4/68-
This means that over and above the eight, there were nine found guilty of capital murder under the old law who received commutation of sentence on that date. The letter continues as follows:
The government decided to get these matters dealt with before the new law got fully under way.
We have really had complete abolition. There is no question but that the government wanted complete abolition, so it could have gone ahead with the economic problems and I am sure this would not have bothered the conscience of any Cabinet member. That is the point I wanted to make.
All arguments and points of view in reference to capital punishment have previously been discussed, stated and restated in this parliament. We have had two lengthy debates. Nothing has changed and nothing new will come out of this debate. Do you think any person will really change his mind after the debate is over or because statistics and figures will be given by various people to support their own viewpoints and special interests, showing increases or decreases or a holding of the line in respect of murder convictions? Murder victims are not mathematical figures; murder victims are human figures and spell human suffering at all levels.
We have had a tremendous amount of statistics. I received a call from the Calgary Herald on January 18, 1973 which indicated there were some statistics left out. I am not going to spend too much time on statistics because my time is limited and I do not want to waste it in this
January 29, 1973

way. I can only draw the conclusion that a breakdown of homicide has been made into 10 or 12 categories. When we look at those categories we must make some deductions. When you lump them together they do not mean very much.
The number of murders in the course of robbery and theft, which is violence, shot up almost 100 per cent during the first three years after the ban. After seven years with fairly level figures, about 65 or 68 killings, there were 119 in the next three years. If you analyse the statistics and motives you will find that murder shot up in numbers in connection with crimes of all kinds; sex crimes and others. The only type of murder where the figures did not go up were those murders caused by passion, generally killings between spouses, which always, as I suggested in my introductory remarks, would be categorized as non-capital murder as a judge would withdraw a different charge from the jury.
I am the first to admit that this subject is a highly emotional and highly controversial one. That is why I was so happy to hear the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly) speak as he did. In this party when we say there will be a free vote, we mean a free vote. There will be no duress on members of this party from anyone. Certainly, we all feel sympathy for an accused awaiting trial and at the time of conviction. I have had experience and I know the feelings of the family, the accused and the community as a result of a conviction. We have sympathy at the time when there is an agonizing waiting period in the penitentiary. You only have to talk to the people who have been in penitentiaries for years to know what kind of a penalty that is.
All of these things after the event tend to work men and women into an emotional frenzy. However, on the other hand, if there were as much emphasis and publicity about some of the monstrous, horrifying and brutal crimes committed against society, the emotional frenzy and sympathy could well run the other way and certainly would be more inflammatory. One only has to consider how the people felt in Vancouver after the Head case.
Let us consider the Head case. This is a man who had been convicted on four different occasions of brutal, sexual assaults on girls between the ages of six and nine years. During the time he was under a life imprisonment sentence he was once declared criminally insane and had the sentence reduced to 15 years. He was released illegally, in my opinion, and I have not time to go into that, and while out of the penitentiary he was accused and found guilty of murdering Tanya Busch, a girl of about six or seven years of age who was the daughter of a prison guard. This apparently was a vendetta against the girl's father.
There are many other cases I could outline and if this bill should go to the committee I hope to deal with them there. I was criticized when I cited the Head case in the House of Commons. The Prime Minister in order to defend his solicitor general, tried to accuse me of linking the two, meaning Head and the victim, prior to the charge of murder. I ignored that remark then and I do so now. My purpose in this debate is to see that society is protect-
25714-47J
Capital Punishment
ed in these cases against administrative asininity. Of course, the minister must take responsibility in this case. The previous minister went on and on and on, and would not stop until finally it became a chronic situation and changes were made. Certainly, we should have rehabilitation of convicted prisoners. I should like to congratulate the new Solicitor General in that regard. It should be remembered that the former solicitor general never understood the priority; that the protection of society must be paramount over rehabilitation and paramount over any other consideration is the protection of society. That is the fundamental matter to be considered in this debate and no other.
I speak from experience. It is not for me to discuss how many times I have been called upon to use my energy and ability to defend those charged with murder. The Solicitor General was teasing me the other day because he had gone to a certain institution and met 12 inmates who had been convicted of murder and who had got a new trial. He was somewhat surprised, but I know something of standing in court with the responsibility of defending people charged with capital and non-capital murder. I mention that only to emphasize that my experience should permit me to speak from the other side of the fence as it were.
Many of my friends suggest that basically I should be an abolitionist, but in the face of violent crime and the lack of consideration for the most precious civil right of all, the right to live within that degree of freedom and liberty that a free society guarantees the individual, I say that the most important civil right is life. I must measure up, therefore, to the responsibility and oppose the bill. Those who obey the law must have rights as well as those who deliberately and violently break the law. If I thought imprisonment was the answer I would support the bill. However, I only have to refer to examples such as the Geoffroy case and the Laporte case to see how much consideration is given to the accused and how little consideration is given to the victims or their relatives, even to the extent that Geoffroy should spend his honeymoon in Spain. I once described it as "going the Goyer way".
The bill flaunts the will of the people of Canada. I dare this government and the abolitionists to test the will of the people on the question of capital punishment by plebiscite. I have started to take my own plebiscite but I did not have time to send out house mail so I advertised asking for a straight yes or no. In the last three days, 996 replies came in from Calgary North asking for the death penalty on planned and premeditated murder but only 70 replies were against it. Total replies were 1066 so that gives me some idea of how people are worked up about the way our society is protected today.
We all dream of a day when society would be safe for the smallest and the frailest. I listened to the hon. member for Ottawa West and I wish to congratulate him on the recent birth of a son. We all reject the law "an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth" and hope that in the 20th century the scaffold will be dead, war will be dead and violence will be dead-but they are very much alive, Mr. Speaker.
Where have we failed in society? Today, we look around us and see that monstruous, planned and deliberate murder is committed and for what purpose? I will deal

January 29, 1973
Capital Punishment
with questions of insanity and provocation in a few minutes, but why are most murders committed? They are committed for power and materialism.
One of the arguments presented by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming) in favour of abolition is the fear of judicial error. Let us talk about that, Mr. Speaker. It would have been more likely to occur prior to 1961 when the definition of murder was changed. The penalties were changed too; for example, life imprisonment for non-capital murder and the death penalty for capital murder. When you have a capital murder case before a judge and jury and the evidence leaves any doubt, not any reasonable doubt but any doubt, in the judge's mind, he reduces the charge to non-capital murder and the jury then only has to decide the question of guilt or innocence. That has been my experience before the high courts in Alberta and Saskatchewan, and I am sure that the judges in the other provinces also understand their responsibility and duty. We have a great judiciary in Canada; our judiciary cannot be compared with that of the United States. Since 1961, few have been convicted of capital murder because where the evidence leaves any doubt-not any reasonable doubt-the judge would withdraw the question of capital punishment from the jury and they would have to decide only on the question of guilt or innocence.
What are some of the defences to murder? Some people believe that if a person has been killed, there has been a homicide. That is not necessarily the case, Mr. Speaker. Let us deal with insanity, Mr. Speaker. Is it any defence? The law of insanity has been more liberally interpreted by the courts. Although parliament has not amended the M'Naghten rule in reference to the law of insanity for 100 years, our knowledge now of diseases such as schizophrenia, paranoia or a combination of both, has increased. From scientific and medical experiments, experts are able to advise the court far better than they did 100 years ago or even ten years ago. The courts have liberally interpreted the section which sets the following test: First, did the aecused know the nature and quality of his act and, second, did he know the act was wrong? In other words, did he know what he was doing and did he know it was wrong? Some people lack social conscience and cannot determine what is right or wrong. I had a case once where one brother shot another on the golf course and, because of something in his environment or make-up, he was declared insane. He did not know that what he was doing was wrong. The law provides protection in such a case.
Provocation is another defence. In my experience, courts are giving a more liberal interpretation of the law where culpable homicide may be reduced to manslaughter if provocation is proven. This is where a reasonable man is provoked beyond what a reasonable man can take. For example, if a man came home and found his wife in bed with somebody else and, without any time elapsing, killed that person, that is not murder but it may be manslaughter.
Last but not least, the courts are now being presided over by younger, more progressive thinking judges and, in consequence, there is a more liberal interpretation of the law. I know when I was a young lawyer some of the judges I appeared before used to make me shake and tremble. Today, the atmosphere is more homey and the
[Mr. Woolliams.J
judicial atmosphere is that justice not only must be done but must be seen to be done.
Life imprisonment and capital punishment have proven to be inadequate with the administration ignoring the Criminal Code which demands that before a person is released there must be an order in council permitting his release. In consequence, these people are released only to duplicate or substitute another crime of violence. I ask hon. members to check their copies of the Criminal Code. Section 684(3) reads:
Notwithstanding any other law or authority, a person in respect of whom a sentence of death has been commuted to imprisonment for life or a term of imprisonment or a person upon whom a sentence of imprisonment for life has been imposed as a minimum punishment, shall not be released during his life or such term, as the case may be, without the prior approval of the Governor in Council.
When our late prime minister, Mr. Pearson, introduced that provision, I thought it was somewhat dangerous because it put the matter in the field of politics. But today, released criminals wander around Just today I was told of a case in Calgary-I will check it out-where a young person was sentenced to 15 years for kidnapping a girl and locking her up in the trunk of a car for a period of seven or eight hours. Now, that offender is going to university, and spends one or two days a week in jail. That is a fine way to get a schooling. If you cannot afford university commit the right crime, such as kidnapping.
In his speech, the minister stressed swift administration of justice. In my opinion, he overlooked one of the most important things, namely, proper punishment. Mr. Justice Mackay of the Court of Appeal of Ontario had something to say about this matter in 1954. He visited prison institutions in the United States, and also at Kingston in Canada. The honourable lady behind me in this party knows something about Kingston, Mr. Speaker. Over the years a few riots have broken out at Kingston. Here is what Mr. Justice Mackay said:
The ultimate justification of any punishment is not alone that it's a deterrent, but that it is the emphatic denunciation by the community of a crime, and from this point of view there are some murders which, because of the enormity of their horror, demand the most emphatic denunciation of all, the death penalty.
He was talking about two young men who had taken an old couple in Northern Ontario and sat them on an electric stove, turned on the burners and tortured them in order to get a few pennies from their pension cheques. The punishment must suit the enormity of the crime. As I say, in 1954 Mr. Justice Mackay had interviewed many prisoners in the United States. Bank robbery was a common crime in those days, and criminals told him on occasion they would not take ammunition with them fearing that if they used guns, and were caught, they might fry. Those were their words.
I am not here to say whether capital punishment is a deterrent, but I agree with the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) in that regard. The most precious civil right is surely the right to life. Today we heard one speech about humanity. The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly) talked about young girls and boys being safe on the streets. Mr. Speaker, I have kept a file on violent crimes over the last two months, violent crimes against
January 29, 1973

children. I hold it in my hand. I do not think the streets are that safe. When we talk about capital punishment being a deterrent I will end with these words, and maybe this is the answer:
There is a rock in a harbour, and upon it a lighthouse is placed to warn ships of the danger. One hears about the ships that run upon the rock in the fog, or during the storm, but one never hears of the ships that passed by in safety.
That is an argument in favour of the deterrent. Who knows how many people capital punishment has deterred from committing murder?

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a previous participant in this debate has remarked that at this stage most of the members have already made up their minds and it is hardly likely their attitudes will be changed in the course of the debate, even by the most eloquent and cogent speeches. For this reason I was inclined to refrain from contributing to the debate, and particularly because I so entirely agree by what was said by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), and also today by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly). However, I have received, as no doubt have other hon. members, a great many letters from individuals and organizations both within my constituency and outside of it, and I did take an active part in the parliament that passed the act of 1967, the partial test ban, which we are now asked to extend for another five years.
I have deeply held convictions on this subject that I would like to express. I would much prefer the final and total abolition of capital punishment, but I will support the partial ban in the present bill as the best available means of moving towards that final and total abolition.
These are moral issues, and questions of fact are involved as well as questions of principle. In my opinion capital punishment, the taking of life by the state, is degrading. Above all, after the most careful study that I have been able to make, I have come to the conclusion that capital punishment is not an effective deterrent and serves no useful purpose.
Many of those who wish to see the return of capital punishment and argue for its retention do so very sincerely, and because of their belief that it is necessary for the protection of society against the gravest of all crimes, the commission of deliberate murder. But in my view this is a mistake.
The great and preponderant weight of the evidence is in favour of the proposition that capital punishment is not an effective deterrent. Mr. Speaker, the matter has been argued over the years in many jurisdictions. I have not the time and I do not want to go into all of them. I was impressed by the statement of Professor Fattah on this matter in his "Study of the Deterrent Effect of Capital Punishment with Special Reference to the Canadian Situation," prepared for the Solicitor General, which has already been cited in parliament by the Solicitor General himself. He concludes that the effectiveness of capital punishment as a deterrent is so limited that its abolition cannot have any serious effect on the incidence of murder.
Capital Punishment
He cites the following limits of deterrence: one, deterrence is irrelevant to the bulk of the population who follow the normal norms of society and whose self-concepts will not permit them to commit crimes, including crimes of murder. Two, deterrence cannot be effective in the case of certain acts of impulsive nature where high emotions or strong motivations are involved. I suspect that they are a very large percentage of the crimes of murder. Three, deterrence cannot be effective for certain categories of criminals such as insane, abnormal, impulsive or compulsive offenders or those consciously or unconsciously seeking to be punished. Four, the death penalty cannot be an effective deterrent for those who are not afraid to die or for those who have a conscious or unconscious desire to die. This includes murderers who commit suicide. Five, deterrence cannot be effective in the cases where punishment can be avoided. I suspect that in the case of most murderers they are satisfied that the punishment can be avoided by their own actions.
I have seen, and I have no doubt most of the members of the House have seen the statistics relating to this question from Europe, Great Britain, and from the various jurisdictions in the United States of America where, I believe, some 11 states have abolished capital punishment. As far as I have been able to determine it is not an even balance. The unquestionable conclusion to be drawn from these actual experiments in the abolition of capital punishment must be that abolition does not in fact increase the rate of crime.
Let us recall that crime was more rife in communities such as Great Britain when capital punishment was a penalty for conviction of petty theft and numerous other offences. Indeed there, when to pickpocket was to commit a crime carrying capital punishment, many people carried on their occupation as pickpockets in the shadow of the gallows, and that is a fairly good illustration, I think, of how capital punishment was a deterrent. When it was proposed to abolish capital punishment in England for the theft of goods worth five shillings or more from a shop, Lord Ellenborough, Chief Justice of the Kings's Bench, said that the repeal of the law and the abolition of the death penalty for stealing goods worth five shillings would cause the most dire consequences, including complete loss of security by homeowners in Britain. The same sort of argument is being used today, and it has the same sort of validity.
There are, of course, much more recent examples. There have been in innumerable studies of the matter by those expert in criminology. The great majority of experts have concluded, as stated by Barnes & Teeters, eminent penologists, in a book entitled, "New Horizons in Criminology", as follows:
History reveals the most varied and numerous proofs that there is no correlation between the severity of the Criminal Code and the infrequency of crime. The statistics that we have available show that there is no ground whatever for holding that the murder rate increases when the death penalty is abolished.
That is stated as a fact by experts and by innumerable people who have taken the trouble to examine the facts.

January 29, 1973
Capital Punishment
Let us deal with the moral issue. Let me quote what the Reverend Archbishop Temple of Great Britain, for whom I have the highest regard and reverence, has written:
I believe that the example of the state taking life, even when it does so in return for life already taken, does more to lower the value of human life in the minds of its citizens than the deterrent influence of this penalty can do to protect the lives of its citizens. In this way I believe that the main influence of the retention of the death penalty is rather to increase than diminish the number of murders.
Those who propose the retention of capital punishment or, indeed, the repeal of the law passed by parliament in 1967 cite facts to show that there has been an increasing number of murders in Canada since the enactment of the legislation abolishing the death penalty, except in the cases of the murder of police officers and prison personnel. What those who cite such figures fail to observe and what is made quite clear in the volume, "Capital Punishment-New Material 1965 to 1972" published under the authority of the former Solicitor General, is that the increase in the rate of that crime has been less than the general increase in the rate of crime in Canada with respect of offences which are not subject to capital punishment. So, even if there is an increase in the rate of murders, that increase is less, apparently, than the common trend of crimes not affected by the existence of capital punishment.
I now want to turn to another item in the book, "Capital Punishment-New Material 1965 to 1972". As mentioned at page 62, the death penalty has been abolished with respect to convictions for rape in Canada. It is of interest to note that at this time, because that law was abolished as long ago as 1955. One would think that if capital punishment had been an effective deterrent with respect to that crime, the abolition of capital punishment would have been accompanied by a substantial rise in the crime rate respecting that particular offence. Exactly the opposite has happened, as shown by the tables. After the death penalty was abolished for that particular offence, the number of offences steadily declined.
I am persuaded, Mr. Speaker, that those most able to recommend on questions involving moral judgment are almost universally in favour of abolition. As recently as November 24, 1972, and may I be pardoned as an Anglican for citing this authority, Archbishop E. W. Scott, Primate of the Anglican Church of Canada, said in a statement to the government that, in his view, the death penalty was immoral as long as there is the faintest possibility that an innocent person might be put to death.
Speaking as a lawyer with some experience in the courts, I know that it is indeed a possibility that an innocent person might be convicted after trial and put to death. In the most advanced jurisdictions of the world there are classic examples of this. The famous Christie case in England is well known because, after an individual was executed for murder, another person confessed to being the guilty party; indeed, it was clear that a miscarriage of justice had resulted. The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) testifies to a clear case of judicial error in a murder case in which he was engaged as counsel.
I have the greatest respect for the courts. I have a lot to do with them. They are a necessary and vital institution in
(Mr. Brewin.]
our society. Nevertheless, the courts are a human institution. It is notorious that, on occasion, they do err. I, myself, have been involved in cases-not, I admit capital cases-in which subsequent new evidence has shown that decisions made and confirmed by courts of first instance and approved by courts of appeal were, in fact, clearly and entirely erroneous. Another case that comes to mind is the famous Truscott case. That case did not involve the finality of execution. On his conviction, as I recall it, Truscott was either 14 or 15 years old. If he had been older he would have been executed and there would have been no possibility of reviewing his case. I studied his case in great detail and it has always been my view that the dissenting judgment of Mr. Justice Hall in the Supreme Court of Canada, in which he held that there had been a mistrial in the Truscott case, was far more convincing than the judgment of the majority of the court.
Archbishop Scott, in the statement I mentioned earlier, went on to say on November 24, 1972:
Since there does not seem to be any conclusive evidence that the death penalty does in fact constitute a deterrent, the present legislation should be retained for at least another five years.
The General Council of the United Church of Canada last month confirmed its stand taken in 1956 for the abolition of the death penalty and now asks the federal government to make such abolition a total, permanent feature of the Criminal Code, as of the expiry date of December 29, 1972.
Social workers are another group with experience in this field. In the province of Ontario, the Ontario Association of Professional Social Workers which represents 1,150 professional social workers supports the abolition of the death penalty. They state:
The issue of the death penalty is really one of ethics and morality. As social workers we feel that the worth and dignity of man is cheapened and lessened by state execution. We are in strong support of the abolition of the death penalty.
There is no lack of high judicial authority on the subject of capital punishment. Quite recently the Supreme Court of the United States, by a five to four verdict, ruled that the death penalty was unconstitutional as it was a breach of the phrase of the Constitution forbidding cruel and unusual punishment. This is a weighty authority in a jurisdiction close to our own and deserves our most careful consideration.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, those countries which can claim the highest measure of social advance have almost exclusively accepted the abolition of the death penalty without serious consequences. I am thinking in particular of the countries of northern Europe, where the murder rates are low and where capital punishment has been abolished for many years. I am thinking of 11 states of the United States of America where the experience has beer, the same. I am thinking of Great Britain, whose social judgments we have often been content to follow in Canada. In that country, after a checkered career, abolition of the death penalty has now been finally accepted. In my view it would be a retrograde step if, indeed, we were to reintroduce the death penalty as the general consequence of conviction for murder.

Hear, hear!
January 29, 1973

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
I am well aware, of course, as are all members of this House, that the crime of murder is often accompanied by a disregard for human life, by brutality and horror which causes, and justly so, moral indignation. It is my view, however, that moral indignation is a poor basis for judgment. Sometimes moral indignation results in a cry for vengeance. The state should not be the instrument for vengeance or retribution. There is the duty, of course, to protect society; but if, as I have said, the protection of society does not require the use of the death penalty, then the state should not use this means.
I am aware from letters I receive that many of my constituents believe the death penalty to be necessary for their security. All I can say, and I say it with all sincerity, is that I believe they are mistaken. I do not know whether in my constituency the majority would like to see the death penalty retained or restored. I am deeply convinced, however, that this is a matter of moral judgment and conviction and that I have no right to shelter behind any theory as to the counting of heads. Ever since the famous speech of Edmund Burke to the Bristol voters, it has been clear that our parliamentary system does not require us to be counters of heads or automatic reflectors of opinion in our constituencies. We are elected to use our own best judgment and to obey our deepest convictions.
I believe, with all the conviction I can muster, that capital punishment does not perform the function claimed by its supporters, nor do I think it can ever be made to serve such a function. It does not protect society. It brutalizes society. It is an archaic custom which has disappeared in most civilized countries. I earnestly hope that this parliament will not take a backward step but rather that it will, perhaps after further delay and further study of statistical evidence, move toward total and final abolition of capital punishment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member who has just spoken. He has given us in such an eloquent way an excellent case for the abolition of what he called a custom which is out of date and which ought to be abolished. It is clear that many of the documents from which the hon. member read are familiar to all of us here, so that in this debate there is bound to be some repetition as we explain to other members of this House and to our constituents why we will cast our votes on this bill in a particular way.
There are those who view the capital punishment debate primarily in terms of its effect on law enforcement and public safety. They argue, correctly I believe, that the prevention of violent crime is one of the most important functions of government, and, indeed, a government which fails to establish and sustain the citizens' safety of life and limb is not worthy of support. Many Canadians today believe hanging should be reintroduced as punishment for murder.
The Gallup poll published on February 2, 1972 asked whether or not the death penalty should be brought back. Of those responding, 63 per cent said yes, bring it back. Of those who favoured reinstatement, 64 per cent cited a rising crime rate as their reason. The heart of the matter, then, seems to be whether or not capital punishment is an
Capital Punishment
effective deterrent against the crime of murder. In certain cases it could so be regarded, as, for example, when a convicted murderer kills again after release from prison. The friends and relatives of victims of such crimes have every reason to feel deeply bitter toward a society which allows a dangerous person to be at large and repeat the criminal act of murder.
In general, however, contrary to popular opinion, there is no clear evidence that the death penalty serves as a deterrent against the committing of murder. In the United States, where the use of the death penalty is determined state by state, there is, in fact, an inverse relationship. The five states with the highest homicide rates all retain the death penalty, while the five with the lowest homicide rates have all abolished the death penalty. Over all, the mean homicide rate in retentionist states is more than double the mean rate in abolitionist states. This, of course, does not prove that retaining the death penalty results in more murders; it simply underscores the difficulty of trying to prove through statistics that the death penalty deters murderers.
The most serious of the social arguments in favour of the death penalty, then, is based on the theory of deterrence. It is claimed that if persons intending to commit crimes know what the punishment will be, they will turn away from committing them. At first glance, this seems to make good sense, but upon closer examination the idea proves less convincing. It has been said that an ordinary person is deterred from crime by comparatively minor penalties. A normal person, if sure of being caught, would refrain from a criminal act out of regard for the consequences. Murderers, however, are surely not normal people. They are abnormal people driven by who-knows-what compulsive forces. Certainly, they are driven sometimes by strong emotional forces, by forces accompanying insanity, even though their particular state of mind at the time may not be legally so defined. In conditions like these, no weighing of consequences takes place within the minds of such persons as they decide to kill. The psychopath will not be deterred by threat of punishment, however severe. Crimes of passion, including violent crimes committed under the influence of drugs such as alcohol, cannot reasonably be assumed to be deterrable by a means such as a death penalty.
If it could be proven that the death penalty was in fact a deterrent-and it cannot be so proved-then, surely, every effort should be made to make the deterrent as effective as possible. As it is now, however, most executions are private affairs rather than public spectacles. Attendance is restricted to the prison warden, a physician, a chaplain and a very few others. Surely, it is illogical to admit to the execution only those who are least in need of such a spectacle to deter them from committing murder.
Why, also, if the death penalty is a deterrent, do we chose a method which is considered to be relatively swift and painless in place of one involving prolonged torture and agony? In Canada, hanging has been accepted as a humane method of execution. In the United States, many states have chosen to electrocute or gas the condemned. If deterrence is the main purpose for imposing the death penalty, then it should not be as humane as possible but,

January 29, 1973
Capital Punishment
rather, slow and agonizing. It should not be a private affair but, rather, a public spectacle.
The bill presently before the House seeks to limit capital murder to cases involving the death of police or prison officers. Those who deal with criminals on a regular basis in the line of duty are unusually susceptible to being murdered. There is no doubt that they ought to receive some special protection, indeed, considerable special protection. It is worth noting, however, that the largest number of police murders, a total of 11, took place in 1962 when capital punishment was still in effect, a year in which two murderers were executed. Since 1962, there have been no executions in Canada; nor has there been an increase in the number of police officers killed in the line of duty. Police work can be extremely dangerous and often is, but there is no evidence to show that having the death penalty in effect makes the working life of a police officer any safer.
It is quite true that there has been an increase in criminal homocide in recent years, but a report from the Solicitor General's department on the deterrent effect of capital punishment, which has been mentioned in several instances in this debate, concludes that the increase cannot be attributed to the suspension of capital punishment. Other violent crimes have also increased, and this situation disturbs and troubles us all. But is the answer to the problem to introduce the death penalty? Is not this simply one more violent reaction to violent action? If we use killing in an effort to prevent killing, then surely this is a sign of despair in our society. It shows that we have no answers to the pressing problem of violent crime and how to prevent it. In addition, capital punishment leaves no room whatsoever for the possible errors of those who sit in judgment on other persons.
I take the stand that the lives of others are not ours to dispose of. The state, in its enforcement of the law against criminal homicide, must not itself permit what amounts to legalized murder. If we appeal to private individuals to refrain from killing, we have just as much right, indeed we have an obligation, also to appeal to the state to refrain from killing.
It should be possible, and I believe that it is possible, to protect society without judicial killing as a sanction. Of course, the public must be satisfied that an individual guilty of murder is given a sentence that is appropriate to his or her crime, considering all the circumstances in each case. The public must be assured that a dangerous criminal is not set free again to threaten our safety. There is surely a need for a better system of deterrence to acts of violence in our society. Certainly, however, the imposition of the death penalty is no such deterrent.
In a five to four decision last June, the United States Supreme Court ruled that the death penalty must be forbidden in almost all cases because it had lost its usefulness. In short, as a deterrent to murder it does not work. I say, then, that we ought to abolish, not in part but outright, the death penalty. When we have done that, we should push on with other social and economic measures which hopefully will be effective in decreasing the resentment and hostility harboured by some of our citizens, for

these are the emotions which may very well in some cases lead to acts of violence, including murder.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF A SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF INQUIRY ON CROWN CORPORATION ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, a special committee of inquiry on Crown corporations exercising financial, commercial or industrial activities be established to study the various Acts establishing such Crown corporations, the Crown Corporations Act sections 76 to 88 of the Financial Administration Act, and all other laws concerning Crown Corporations and to recommend to the House the adoption of a law regarding federal public enterprises; the committee should also study the following subjects without restrictions (a) the legal rules pertaining to the employees of such corporations (b) their financial structure (c) the way in which they are financed (d) government control over said corporations (e) fiscal regulations (municipal, school, provincial and federal taxes, (f) the status of the administrators (g) the privileges of such corporations resulting from their being "commissioned by Her Majesty" (h) the status of the subsidiaries of these enterprises (i) their purchasing policy (j) the problem of auditing by the Auditor General of Canada or by private auditors (k) the appropriateness of State intervention in the economic field in the form of enterprises; and all other matters concerned.
Mr. Speaker, once again I am introducing this motion concerning Crown corporations and I would like to draw the attention of the House on three specific facts.
January 29, 1973

Firstly, Crown corporations are creatures of the Government and, as such, of Parliament itself, each one with a specific field of activity. Now, the only information we get as members of Parliament on those corporations is summarized in their respective annual reports. Finally, parliamentary control is just about nonexistent. This I will try to show in a little while.
Secondly, the government to-day, in Canada, ownes and operates about a hundred industrial, commercial or financial corporations the assets of which are in excess of $20 billion. This modern phenomenon of governments involved in business undertakings give rise to many problems especially where parliament and parliamentary control over such corporations are concerned. For instance who will tell me what is the status to-day of a government involved in business dealings? Will it be subject to private law or public law? Will it be given a mixed status and be made subject to both private and public law? What kind of control has parliament over these Crown corporations? How is it that the Auditor General of Canada, who is a parliament employee appointed by parliament cannot audit the books of all these Crown corporations?
For MPs, the main sources of information on Crown corporations are their annual report, written questions on the order paper, and the tabling of documents. We shall see how efficient each of these may be. Why is parliament opposed, through the government, to creating a committee on Crown corporations so that members may control their operations?
Those are questions which warrant consideration since, in this House, Crown corporations are now a forbidden subject. Nobody dares mention them. What means of control do we have over the Crown corporations? They amount to just about nothing. The corporations do send us their annual reports which, and everybody will agree with me, are put away on the shelves to collect dust.
To my mind, normally or ideally, those reports should be referred to a parliamentary committee on public corporations. In a way, such a committee would act as a shareholders' meeting and the members could control the various activities of those companies.
The written questions offer the hon. members another opportunity of obtaining information on Crown corporations. The written questions are those the members put on the order paper. Anybody knows that. They can be technical. However, I would remind my hon. colleagues that in all cases, the minister may decline to answer a question on the order paper without stating his reason for doing so, and it is even against the Standing Orders of the House to insist on getting an answer; furthermore, no debate is allowed under those conditions. In this regard, I refer my colleagues to Citation 181(3), page 158 of Beauchesne's Rules and Forms, 4th edition. In other words, neither annual reports nor questions on the order paper have any value as far as parliamentary control is concerned.
Mr. Speaker, that is why I am bringing forward the motion before us in order that members of Parliament may exercise some control, be aware of what is happening in Crown corporations, and report to the people of
Crown Corporations
Canada on the activities of some hundred Crown corporations handling over $20 billion of the taxpayers' money.
Mr. Speaker, it quite frequently happens that the management of such an agency or the minister in charge refuse to reply to our questions. In fact when a member of Parliament makes an inquiry of a minister or writes to a Crown corporation, inquiring about one area or another, on many occasions he receives negative replies. That is what I particularly want to object to.
For instance, I am concerned with the problem of internal management. A public agency is under no obligation to reply to a question concerning internal management, yet the appointment of personnel of a public agency is solely a responsibility of management. One can make any kind of patronage one wishes. Management never discloses information from the personal files of officers and employees. Also, and I quote:
It is not customary to ask Crown corporations . .. information about their employees or other matters of internal management.
This is why it was so difficult last year, as much for me as for the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Bicul-turalism, to learn how many employees of each one of these corporations were bilingual, how many had English or French as their mother tongue, what were their salaries. It is a nonsense to tolerate such a situation.
If a member of Parliament wants to inquire about the salaries of the employees of these hundred or so Crown corporations, what will happen? A public corporation will not answer a question either about the salary of an employee or of a group of employees. The answer will be:
.. . salaries are deemed confidential.
I would refer you to the order paper of October 23, 1963, more precisely to question No. 1246. Regarding salaries, the late Hon. Guy Favreau, then Minister of Justice, said, and I quote:
Let us note here that in the Public Accounts, while the individual salary of every public servant paid more than a certain amount is listed, the salaries of employees of a Crown corporation are grouped under a single item. It is practically only through a question directed in the House to the responsible minister that the salary of an officer or an employee of a Crown corporation will be known if it pleases the minister to divulge it.
Then again, may I remind the House of the citation of parliamentary procedure which I quoted earlier, so that the hon. member still cannot get the requested information.
Again recently, the C.B.C. stated through its responsible minister, and I quote:
... it is not the Corporation's policy to divulge the salary paid to an individual.
With regard to fees, any public corporation will also refuse to disclose what it pays to an individual.
This is what appears on page 4975 of Hansard for December 4, 1967:
-The Corporation is not usually required to disclose the fees paid to any particular person.
Identical replies were given to questions Nos. 1,713 and 1,868 of December 4 and 18, 1963.
Each time the minister gave exactly the same answer so that one can conclude that CBC is protected by the minis-
742

January 29, 1973
Crown Corporations
ter; he is authorized to refuse to answer if he feels like it so that any member, whether on the government side or on the opposition side, has absolutely no control and cannot get information in any way.
On the subject of the contract awarded following a call for tenders the public firm will refuse-
-to disclose the name of the companies or persons submitting tenders or to give information on the tenders received.
And that at almost any time.
One could also talk about internal studies. It could be interesting sometimes for a member to know the studies made by experts within a given Crown corporation. Those studies, one must admit again, are paid for by the taxpayers.
There again it was decided, and I quote:
-it is contrary to custom ... to disclose the names of persons assigned to studies.
The firm considers those studies to be-
-private documents-
-for the internal use of the firm.
I could refer you to the debates of the House of Commons of February 26, 1969, page 5969. One could also talk about the salary of the president and general manager of a corporation. One can read there:
It is customary not to disclose any information from personal files of civil servants and employees and this custom was supported by the Sessional Committee on Railways and Shipping.
I will refer now to page 5665 of the Debates of December 20, 1967 and page 6387 of the Debates of March 10, 1969.
Mr. Speaker, that answer was given by Air Canada, Northern Transport Corporations Limited, Eldorado Nuclear Limited, Cape Breton Development Corporation and by Polymer Corporation Limited. Nevertheless, the Canadian National, the Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation, the CBC, the CHMC, and the SACE revealed the salary of their chief executive. So there is no established or well defined practice there either.
All that may somewhat bore some of my colleagues but it is nonetheless an extremely important matter. In concluding, I will only call their attention to this: It is a well known fact that a large industrial, commercial and financial area is owned and operated today by the federal government. I will say for the benefit of my colleagues, that the government operates uranium mines, like Eldorado Nuclear Limited, coal mines, like Cape Breton Development Corporation, is carrying out mining exploration through SOQUEM and oil exploration through the Panarctic Oils Limited. The government operates one of the world's largest railway systems with the Canadian National Railways Company. It owns several road transport corporations with the Canadian National Transportation Limited. It operates the most important hotels in Canada with the Canadian National Hotels Limited. It is involved in air transport with Air Canada and Eldorado Aviation Limited as well as maritime transport with the Canadian National and Northern Transportation Corporation Limited.

The State, the federal government, is also one of the largest rubber producers in the world, with Polymer Corporation Limited; it owns and operates one of the largest radio and television systems, namely the CBC, it produces and sells electricity with Hydro-Quebec, Ontario Hydro etc. It grants interest bearing loans through the Industrial Development Bank, the CMHC, the Farm Credit Corporation, the Deposit and Investment Fund, etc. In brief the state owns and operates today more than one hundred of those corporations and thus administers more than $20 billion of the taxpayers' money in goods and capital.
The purpose of the motion I introduced is to urge this House to create a committee to study all factors related to the administration of these corporations. Why is the Auditor General of Canada not allowed to audit the accounts of these corporations? I could refer my colleagues to a question which I asked in the House and that I had to put on the Order Paper. Finally, this question was answered after pressures were put on the minister. I was told that for this or that Crown corporation, the books were audited by a Toronto company, made up of friends of the party in power, etc.
Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General of Canada is the only public officer commissioned by Parliament to audit accounts. I do not understand why this person whom the government does not like but who however has authority, could not audit the books of these corporations on behalf of Parliament. I do not understand why hon. members, who have been elected by their constituents, could not have the privilege and right to sit on a parliamentary committee on Crown corporations, for instance, in order to know the administration, the policy, the investments of such corporations, etc.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the motion will not only get the attention of my colleagues from all parties in this House, but most of all their support, so that Parliament finds a way to control the Crown corporations and thus account for them to the population in a more efficient way.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF A SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF INQUIRY ON CROWN CORPORATION ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the notice of motion proposed by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) is similar to a notice of motion standing on the order paper in my name and one on which I spoke a few years ago. In fact, his notice of motion goes further than mine. Mine simply suggested that there should be at least one member of parliament on each of the boards of directors of crown corporations in order to have closer control over the spending of government that takes place through the crown corporations. The hon. member for Lotbiniere suggests that perhaps a special committee of the House could be established to look into all aspects of crown corporations. I think this is a good idea, although I do not necessarily agree with all the details the hon. member has mentioned. This is something which is long overdue.
We come here as representatives of the people but are unable to represent them because we have absolutely no say over most of the spending of government which takes place through crown corporations. Even the minister has very little to say in the matter because these corporations have become completely autonomous, and it is a bad thing to suggest political interference. Who represents the
January 29, 1973

people of Canada if not the Members of Parliament? We should be looking into these matters; indeed, it is our duty to do so yet we are being thwarted at every turn because the Mandarins have built into their organizations so much autonomy and so much independence from the elected representatives. They are trying to head us off at the pass because we have been asking that control be given back to those who were elected. I can give a very good example of this.
Certain bills which are being prepared by the Mandarins propose to include members of the public service on the boards of directors instead of Members of Parliament. They want to keep us as far away as possible whilst retaining and adding to the power that they already have. This is the case in the Air Canada Act which is being prepared at the present time. Until recently even Air Canada had nothing to say about it because the Mandarins were writing themselves into the act as members of the board of directors. Are we going to stand for this kind of thing?
I believe that the hon. member's suggestion that a special committee be formed is an excellent one. Most of our crown corporations report to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) for Canada and that minister exercises certain statutory powers over some, such as the CBC, CRTC, Canadian Film Development Corporation and the National Museum. However, he is not responsible for the management of them. The role of the minister with regard to some of the other agencies is as spokesman to the House. If we ask a question of the minister in the House, all he can say is that he will refer it to the corporation in question and bring back their answer. In other words, responsibility concerning the management of most of the corporations and agencies under the jurisdiction of the minister does not rest directly upon his shoulders. Consequently, he has no direct control over their activities in spite of the fact that the over-all policy is supposed to be a policy of the government.
In this regard, Mr. Speaker, there are some Crown corporations which have been making policy, although in my view this should not be the role of a Crown corporation. Policy should be made by the government. The merits of independence from the executive power have been questioned by many people on the grounds that any agency which spends public funds should be answerable to a public official who, in turn, must be responsible ultimately to parliament. On the other hand, those who argue in favour of the greatest possible independence of these agencies from the executive power claim that these institutions must have a freedom of action which will keep them outside the political sphere completely, so that they can fulfil their obligations and duties objectively and without partisanship.
With regard to the question of keeping outside the political sphere and being non-partisan and objective, Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that when you get patronage from public servants, it is far worse than any patronage from politicians. The argument that is used is the sensitive one regarding freedom of expression and thought, particularly with respect to the CBC. Government control of the CBC would infringe on freedom of expression and thought, of course, but it seems to me that there is a great
Crown Corporations
deal of difference between control by the government and the other extreme which is abuse or licence and which really cannot be called freedom at all.
The government has several solutions at its disposal. For example, it can name the president of the CBC and it has control over the budget which goes before the committee. In theory I suppose the minister could tell the committee not to approve the budget but, of course, this simply is not done. It would be tantamount to a vote of non-confidence in the government.
Another more difficult problem is the question of control over corporations and agencies by this parliament. Parliament must authorize funds and expenditures. Of course, it could refuse but I have never known this to happen and I do not think it would be a very good idea to refuse funds already approved by the Treasury Board and which have very likely been spent. So, we are beaten before we start in that respect as well. There have been many complaints on the part of Members of Parliament, as well as by the public, and there has been an expression of frustration on the part of Members of Parliament. We represent the people. Therefore, we naturally feel that we should have some say in how the moneys of the people are spent. Yet under the present system when moneys are misappropriated by Crown agencies, the representatives of the people are helpless in stopping such practices.
I agree that it is a ticklish problem to determine where control should be applied. On the one hand, agencies should be free of political intervention if they are to function properly, but they must be kept aware of the fact that the funds are supplied by the people of Canada. The only control possible would be through the representatives of the people in parliament. This is the reason I have repeatedly suggested that on the board of directors of each of the Crown corporations and agencies there should be at least one Member of Parliament. This does not necessarily mean a member from the government side of the House. In fact, in the case of the CNR and the CBC these are large enough agencies that they could have more than one Member of Parliament on their boards, perhaps a member from the government side and a member from one of the opposition parties. This would ensure some kind of political in-put.
When I say political in-put, I am not talking about partisanship. These members would act as watchdogs over the spending of those corporations. Mr. Speaker, I have raised this matter on several occasions in the House, and on one occasion I had a concrete example given to me. Since I have not had the chance to ask for the hon. member's permission, that is, of the hon. member who wrote me this letter, I shall not quote it but merely paraphrase it.
This Member of Parliament ran into a very difficult situation when a Crown corporation laid off a number of men and advised him only the night before the announcement was to be made. Here was a case where the hon. member had several arguments that he could have presented. He was not able to do so because he only knew after the fact. As a result, many people were out of work because of the decision taken by the board of that Crown
25714-48i

January 29, 1973
Crown Corporations
corporation. There is no doubt that other means could have been employed such as that political in-put which I have suggested by someone who understands the situation from the people's point of view, someone who represents those people here in this House. Here is a case where that hon. member felt that if he, or another political person, had been on the board of directors of that corporation this unfortunate situation could have been avoided.
So, Mr. Speaker, perhaps the idea of having Members of Parliament on the boards of directors is one of the things that should be considered by a committee. Therefore, I like the idea that the hon. member has put forward. The committee could be made up of members from both sides of the House, as are all our committees. It could go from place to place in order to decide what is the best course to follow to give us more control over these bodies.
A while ago I mentioned the Crown corporations coming under the Secretary of State. There are many others as well. There is the CNR, for example. The pages and pages that have been put into Hansard on that subject show that there is a great deal of dissatisfaction in the country with the way the CNR is handled. Perhaps a little more in-put from this House would help that situation. And we have people who are capable of doing these things, people who know just as much about railroads as people who are presently on the board of the CNR.
Air Canada is another Crown corporation which should be studied and looked at from various points of view. A committee of this kind could look at the various questions concerning Air Canada. From time to time we have heard suggestions that Air Canada should not be strictly a Crown corporation, that it should be owned only partially by the government, say, 50 per cent or 60 per cent, and partially through public shares. This is something that could be looked at by the suggested committee. We have heard another suggestion that CP and Air Canada should be amalgamated, and thereby have only one international airline for Canada. It is a suggestion that has merit and could be examined by a special committee such as this. There are all kinds of subjects that could be looked at by such a committee.
The government does not have to adopt everything the committee recommends, but the government would be in a position to judge much better the various problems which it does not have the time to examine itself. A special committee of the House could certainly provide the basic necessities, and bring the various studies together. Many studies have been made of different subjects, but the reports are lying about all over the place. They have never been co-ordinated, and one weighed against another, to determine the best course for Canadians.
I terminate with these words, Mr. Speaker, that although I still believe there should be Members of Parliament on the boards of Crown corporations, I should like to say that I am even more excited about the idea of a special committee which could look into not only that aspect but several other aspects of the affairs of Crown corporations.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF A SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF INQUIRY ON CROWN CORPORATION ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter that is before us during this private member's hour is an interesting one, although when you look

at the terms of the motion before us you find that it is a verry broad one indeed. The hon. member says that he wants a special committee of inquiry on Crown corporations, and the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart) as well as the hon. member who moved the motion, seemed to imply that it is to be a special committee of this House. However, as I look upon the motion that is before us, I see that it could be much broader than that in its terms. It could include a special committee such as is brought in for other inquiries. I could think of the Rand Inquiry with respect to certain matters. I could think of the Bryden Committee, one formed for public service matters which, like so many other committees formed by the government, has never yet reported despite the repeated requests of members of this House.
There are many kinds of committees that could be envisaged within the terms of the motion. Unfortunately, the terms of reference are not clear as to what kind of committee the House would be dealing with in the event that it saw fit to pass the motion. However, the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) asked a very fundamental question with respect to Crown corporations. He asked: what business has the state in the business field? As I pondered that question I was looking at a document called "The Government of Canada Programs and Services" issued in July, 1972, by CCH Canada Limited. On page 417 of that document there is an appendix which sets forth certain Crown corporations. The list is intended to be exhaustive, but from what the hon. member says I am satisfied that there are many more than appear on this list.
I return now to the question of what business has the state in the business field. When one reads about the various types of Crown corporations, one can see how the state or government has entry into the business world, under the guise of a Crown corporation, in a way that is somewhat frightening. A Crown corporation, Mr. Speaker, is a form of public enterprise which has become increasingly important as this type of institution has developed. As you know, Sir, Crown corporations are established and regulated under the Financial Administration Act which defines a Crown corporation as a corporation that is accountable to parliament, through the minister, for the conduct of its affairs.
Generally speaking, there are three classes of Crown corporations. First, there is the departmental corporation which is a servant or agent of Her Majesty in right of Canada and is responsible for the administration, regulation or supervision of activities that are governmental in nature. I do not think there is much difficulty with that kind of Crown corporation or any problem with respect to intrusion into the private sector.
Second is the corporation which is an agent of Her Majesty in right of Canada and is responsible for the management of trading or surplus operations on a semicommercial basis, or for management, procurement, construction or disposal activities on behalf of Her Majesty in right of Canada. That kind of corporation, I think, has intruded into the business life of the community. Then there is the other type of corporation known as the proprietary corporation, which is responsible for the manage-
January 29, 1973

ment of lending or financing operations or for the management of commercial and industrial operations involving the production or the dealing in of goods and the supply of services to the public. The agency corporation normally is required to conduct its operations without federal appropriations. Whether Crown corporations conduct their operations with or without federal appropriations, they are none the less those kinds of corporations that bring themselves within the parameters of the question posed by the mover of the motion before the House.
Certainly, when there is an intrusion into business life and, more importantly, when this intrusion is occasioned on money provided from the public purse, there ought to be some agency set up for the control of those expenditures, to monitor the activities of those corporations and organizations. Two types of agencies have been suggested in this debate. The first is a special committee of this House or perhaps of both Houses. I hesitate to make this suggestion because the other place has suffered somewhat at the hands of this House. Such a committee is one suggestion. By this means there could be a reporting from time to time on a regular basis and the opportunity to call witnesses. Actually, Mr. Speaker, we have such rights at the moment.
I am a new member of this parliament. I first came to this chamber of January 4, 1973. Before coming I read, in preparation, some committee proceedings involving an agency of government, the National Capital Commission, which is near and dear to my heart and to those in the constituency I have the honour to represent. That commission came before a committee of this House to have its estimates examined. The chairman of the commission, Mr. Douglas Fullerton, and the responsible minister through whom that commission reports to this House were examined by members of the committee composed of representatives from all sides of the House. In other words, I wanted to know how much was being paid to the miners and how much to people employed on managerial functions. I was told there were 246.25 hourly-paid employees and 141.25 salaried employees. So they divide people into quarters. I also found that the wages of salaried employees were roughly $1,454,000 and the wages of hourly-rated employees totalled approximately $2,591,000. The rub comes in question No. 6 which is as follows:
What was the cost of producing a pound of uranium oxide for each of the past ten years?
The answer I received was rather frustrating:
The requested information is of a proprietary nature, the disclosure of which would be prejudicial to the Company's-and the public's-interests in light of the competitive position of Eldorado Nuclear Limited in marketing uranium on a worldwide basis.
So be it: that information is not available to me. Looking further into the question of financial statements, there
January 29, 1973

is another company that is sort of an offshoot of Eldorado Nuclear, called Eldorado Aviation Limited; they published a balance sheet as well. Eldorado Nuclear also operates a store in Uranium City and it gouges pretty stiff prices out of the miners. According to the 1970 annual report of Eldorado Nuclear, Eldorado played a major role in the development of this fledgling industry by making available its knowhow in the prospecting, mining and metallurgical fields, as well as by negotiating and administering contracts for the sale of uranium by private producers to agencies of the United States and United Kingdom governments. By 1958 there were 25 producing mines in Canada and the peak output of almost 31 million pounds was attained the following year. This Crown corporation was the first uranium producing mine in Canada.
