subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, much has been written and said on the subject of capital punishment. Yet there is one aspect of this vital and perplexing problem which has been little considered or discussed. I trust it could prove to be the basic premise on which hon. members' final decision on the validity of capital punishment will be made.
Capital punishment, it has been established, is the execution of a criminal pursuant to a sentence of death imposed by a competent court. Whatever may have been its origin, whether in feelings of revenge as described by the lex talionis, the law of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, or in theories of retribution or deterrence, capital punishment is a term opposed to all irregular modes of punishment, such as the American "lynch law" or any modern survival of "blood avengers".
Capital punishment is so named from the Latin, caput, because hanging or decapitation was the most usual mode of death. In England, during Saxon times, man-slaying demanded the payment of what was known as "wer-gild" or ."blood money", the amount of which varied with the degree of importance in the social scale of the murdered person.
In pre-Norman times there were various forms of capital punishment, including hanging, decapitation, burning, and hurling from rocks after the manner of the Roman custom of throwing malefactors from the classic Tarpeian Rock. After the conquest mutilation seems to have been substituted and this is the punishment mentioned in assizes of the time of Henry II. The law was variable for some time after that but gradually crystallized into such a condition that capital punishment became the common penalty for a great number of crimes, comprising treason and all felonies except larceny and mayhem.
This state of things continued to 1826, at which time there were nominally no fewer than 200 crimes punishable by death. Subsequently in England the only capital offences were treason, murder, piracy with violence, and the crime of setting fire to His Majesty's vessels of war, arsenals, military or naval stores and ships in the port of London. The sentence of capital punishment could also be passed by courts martial in various cases of mutiny, desertion or sleeping on sentry duty.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel).]
In conformity with his general theory of punishments and reward, that the evil of punishment must not exceed the advantage to the offender, and that punishment should be exactly and mathematically proportioned to the offence, Jeremy Bentham proposed abolishing the death penalty in most cases, retaining it only for murder and treason, and this is a royal commission which submitted its report in 1866 recommended. In Canada, under the Criminal Code of 1906 only treason, murder, piracy with violence, and rape were capital crimes.
Arguments for or against the death penalty in all ages have been of two kinds. Some are categorical assertions based on traditional sentiment and beliefs. The claims that man's innate sense of justice requires that a murderer should lose his own life, or that man has no right to take life, fall into this class. There is another class of arguments which are empirical in nature. They mainly focus on the belief that capital punishment has a unique power to deter people from committing crimes.
It has been well established by statistical studies that: first, when comparisons are made between contiguous states with similar populations and similar social, economic and political conditions, homicide rates are the same and follow the same trend over a long period of time regardless of the use or non-use of capital punishment; second, the abolition, introduction or reintroduction of this penalty is not accompanied by the effect on homicidal rates that is postulated by the advocates of capital punishment; third, even in communities where the deterrent effect should be greatest because the offender and his victim lived there and the trial and execution were well publicized, homicide rates are not affected by the execution; and fourth, the number of policemen killed by criminals is no higher in abolition states than in comparable death penalty states.
Capital punishment, then, does not appear to have a specific influence on the number or trend of the kinds of crime it is supposed to deter people from committing, and its non-use is not followed by a significant upswing in the rate of these crimes. Modern thought, though, strongly concludes that there are types of murder which should be punished with the death penalty. These are: the killing of a policeman or jail guard who because of the nature of his occupation is exposed to being killed, and being the guardians of society they merit the most protection which we can give them; murder for profit or gain; murder during the commission of a crime or as the result thereof, and multiple murder, such as placing a bomb in a school, airplane or public place, or in the mail addressed to a person.
In April, 1966, an attempt was made to achieve complete abolition but it was rejected on a free vote in this House. In 1967, the same parliament passed for a five-year trial a law which has a compromise and which abolished hanging for all but the murderer of prison guards and policemen. This law, as we all know, expired at the end of 1972.
The profound question, then, that immediately faces hon. members in the twenty-ninth parliament is: Are you in favour of the death penalty for murder, or are you not? Perhaps you are one who on religious grounds believes that under no circumstances should life be taken, either by an individual or by the state. In this case, your vote is
January 29, 1973

already decided. Perhaps you hold that society is becoming progressively more lawless and that the death penalty should be extended to more crimes than murder. If so, there are many precedents in history for your stern conviction.
Perhaps you will turn to statistics and try to prove to yourself that either one course or the other is correct. Your decision may depend upon the age, the civilization or the political climate at the time the events underlying the statistical data took place. You may turn to philosophical thought, to prominent moralists or or even to mystical essays to lift your mind out of the morass of indecision in which you flounder.
You may turn to the law and follow its developing course over the centuries and, by hewing strictly to the line, fashion out of solid timber your final judgment. You may find that the attitude to the death penalty is, by the nature of the flux of society, variable. You may have read that in certain countries in times of peace and affluence the death penalty was not considered necessary, but that in the same countries under the rule of a Hitler or a Mussolini or a Stalin capital punishment was used to its full extent.
You may argue that the executions of innocent persons have undoubtedly occurred, even though rarely. You may bolster your argument with the indisputable fact that the trend toward abolition has continued down the years to grow in the peacetime codes of many nations. You may appeal to all the authorities of your own and earlier times and, as they almost invariably have done, you may overlook the one aspect of this sombre problem which might point you to an altogether human and logical answer.
Should a man who has wilfully killed another man, himself be killed? Historically, this question has been asked of those living after the event. The prosecuting attorney pleads it in his implacable argument before judge and jury. The defence attorney denies it in his impassioned plea for the life of the murderer. The judge juggles the question in his summing up to their jury. And the jury deliberates on it, sometimes in anguish, sometimes in great clarity of mind. Yet in all that has been written and said on the subject of capital punishment, seldom has anyone questioned what the victim would say about it if only he could. And, after all, equally with his murderer, the victim has the right of say in the matter of his own death and its punishment.
It is preached, and rightly, that love, the highest of human emotions, should pe practised impartially in a society. It is a political dogma in our own country that equality is the right of all men. That the punishment should fit the crime is the assiduous desire of all lawmakers and of the law itself. Yet this love and this equality and this minute balancing of the law almost invariably are applied to the living. The victim, the dead man, is almost universally forgotten.
At the split second before his death, the victim-to-be has a moral and constitutional right to equality with his murderer. The love that flourishes in the land has an equal demand on the two of them. Equality and love must be equal, else the fabric of society is torn. In this split second
Capital Punishment
before his death, the victim, above all others, has the right to cry out, "Do as you would be done by!" It is to this split second that judge and jury and attorneys and hon. members should look when assessing the rightness of capital punishment.
It is in the law that, if a man comes into your home with his fists clenched to assault you, you may take the requisite steps to defend yourself. You may not go beyond what is necessary to beat him back. You may not take the samurai sword off your wall and run him through. But you may employ equal force to his. Supposing the victim-to-be of a premeditated murder were to know in a flash of insight exactly what was in the mind of his assailant; suppose everything were equal; suppose the victim-to-be had a gun in his hand at the same instant as his murderer approached him with gun in hand. What would be the inalienable right of the threatened man?
What would you do if you were the victim-to-be? Would you simply stand there and allow him to shoot you through the heart? If so, you would voluntarily relinquish your equality before the law and your right to the love of the land. Would you turn and run? Then you would be a coward. Or would you employ equal force to his and shoot him dead? If the majority of hon. members are of the last opinion, then the vote is already in on the question of capital punishment.
The trouble is, the rights of the victim are often overlooked in the hurly-burly of the trial of his murderer. All the attention is fixed on the plight of the man on trial. Safe in their own comfortable homes, remote from the confrontation which took place at the moment of a man's death, people are prone in the intervening months to sympathize with this living man who is, after all, one of them and must merit mercy. They forget that the dead victim received neither sympathy nor mercy.
In effect, judge and jury and populace-all, to some extent, are accomplices after the fact in the murder of the victim. Society, after the crime, does not feel threatened and therefore can afford the luxury of pity for the killer and an inclination toward leniency. Instead, society should stand as a surrogate for the victim, stepping into his shoes in that split second before his death and deciding, with the wisdom of aftersight, what he would have done in the face of his murderer. And, in effect, I ask hon. members, what would you have done?

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many excellent speeches have been given on the subject that we are now debating. It is a most controversial bill that is before us, yet a most important one. Certainly it is important to a convicted murderer who may be condemned to death as a result of this debate. It is important to all Canadians who want to do their very best for Canada in so far as it affects the safety of all of its citizens. A country which is not ruled by fair laws and guarantees justice for all is in trouble indeed.
May I first pay my compliments to various members, particularly the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), who are opposed to capital punishment. I respect their views and the sincerity with which they are presented, but I do not share them. Without any twang of conscience whatsoever. I tell you that under certain circumstances I am for capi-

January 29, 1973
Capital Punishment
tal punishment and I hope that the present bill before us is defeated. My feelings can be summed up in one statement. Where any country begins to think more of the criminal than it does of the victim, then that country is indeed in a horrible state of affairs.
My concern and where I ask that capital punishment be reinitiated in Canada is where it applies to the first degree murderer. The individual who kidnaps a little girl and finally strangles her, the man who shoots a bank teller, the man who over a period of months poisons his wife, the individual who puts a time bomb in a plane and consequently kills dozens of innocent people; this is the type of crime that I describe as first degree murder. Let us not forget, too, the professional killer, the man who kills for a price. These examples are premeditated murder and criminals of this nature, many of whom have been in and out of jail many times, should be eliminated from society.
Are my hon. friends suggesting that law and order have not deteriorated in the past five years? If they are, then they should start reading the papers. Let us for a moment look at that great country to the south of us. Last year there were ten times as many murders in New York city as there were in Canada, twice as many in Detroit as in our country. It is not safe, Mr. Speaker, to walk down the streets of those two cities by oneself because of muggings and other crimes of violence, and the same can be said of other American cities. Thank heaven that we have not yet reached that stage in Canada, but we would be fools not to admit that it could happen right here if our laws are not enforced much more stringently than they are at present.
The average Canadian criminal is now, if he knows his way through the system, all but able to escape meaningful punishment. He can plead psychological unfitness, economic deprivation, drug abuse, alcohol use, poor social environment, and first conviction for a particular crime as mitigating circumstances. Once sentenced he has his day, parole, compassionate leave, holidays, automatic remissions, good behaviour, and the Lord only knows what else, which reduces his time in prison, if such has been the sentence, to about one half of the sentence imposed.
It is no wonder today that people do not understand the courts and the judicial system. The man in the street is quickly losing faith in justice. The officials in society seem to be on the side of the criminal. Crime rates rise, not because of social or economic condition but because persons realize that little or nothing happens to them even when convicted. Certainly capital punishment will stop few from committing murder. However, re-establishing capital punishment, and in fact more strict punishment in general for social crimes, will restore greater faith in our judicial system. It will give greater vitality to persons who wish to lead good lives; it will give people a greater sense of security. Society will benefit. The old concept of reward and punishment will not be a relic of the past. It will reverse the too often criminal trend of our present society.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) tells us there is now compensation for victims of crimes. One could ask the Solicitor General through you, Mr. Speaker, how one
(Mr. Whicher.]
compensates the victim of a murderer. The most that we could do is to pray for such a victim; he or she has passed all other compensation.
It is interesting to note that practically all guards and practically all policemen are for capital punishment. These are the people who really come into contact with all criminals, including murderers. Policemen are not fools, they are not pigs and they are not fuzz. They are men and women who are average Canadians like those of us here, who have accepted the dangerous job of making life for all citizens a better and a safer one. But, Mr. Speaker, many criminals are laughing at the police today. They scorn them and, as a matter of fact, in many instances society takes the side of the criminal and not the police. Deny it if you wish, but it is a fact.
May I ask you, Mr. Speaker, why a policeman should risk his life against an armed criminal who may kill him and then get out of jail in eight or ten years? Why should a guard in a penitentiary face men known as lifers who have nothing to lose? They are supposedly incarcerated for life, and if they kill one guard or ten they cannot be punished more than now. The cards are stacked against the guards. A dog is supposed to be man's best friend, and yet there are some dogs that become mad and must be destroyed. Unfortunately, we have some men who become mad also and they, too, must be destroyed for the sake of society.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I add that I believe such murderers should be eliminated as painlessly as possible. Perhaps a tranquillizing pill and a shot of gas would be the answer for those people who claim that capital punishment is a matter of vengeance. Let us not forget that the vast majority of Canadian citizens conscientiously believe that capital punishment for first degree murder should be reinitiated. Let us as Members of Parliament represent the views of those who sent us here in the first place. Capital punishment must come back where the criminal, beyond a shadow of doubt, has committed first degree murder. It will make Canada a safer and a better place in which to live.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with a popular and emotional issue.
This is why the Canadian people are extremely eager to know what will be the decision of their representatives. Such an issue, where indeed the right to live of some citizens is at stake, is very difficult and the members are reduced to a dilemma since some of them can quite conscientiously object to the death penalty while they know quite well that such is not the feeling of their constituents.
This is a real dilemma as we realize when hearing the members who state their views. Is the role of the member restricted to that of voicing a personal view or must he express the opinion of the people who elected him to do so? This the question to which we must reply. We should in that regard consult the public opinion which is well known. In the constituency I have the honour to represent I know-because I inquired in this connection-over 90 per cent of the population endorse capital punishment.
What makes citizens in general basing themselves decide in favour of capital punishment? Sure, there are a

great many reasons ranging from simple revenge to instinctive reaction to inflict upon the murderer the same fate that he inflicted on his victim. This is an instinctive and normal reaction. But if you put yourselves in the shoes of the relatives or friends of the victims, you can undersand their instinctive reaction of insisting that the ultimate penalty be inflicted on the murderer.
Those who have known people who were accused of murder and were not guilty favour the abolition of the death penalty.
What is the major argument put forward by the public? It is for a would-be murderer the fear of knowing that he could be executed. Recent surveys and statistics tended to prove that this fear is practically non-existent. People often base their arguments on the following principle: Society cannot allow itself to do precisely what it blames someone for doing.
Mr. Speaker, people also say that in a modern society there ought not to be inhuman punishment, and they point to changes which have taken place through the years. One might be inclined to agree with those who base their arguments on the reasoned and reasonable principle that society should not allow itself to do what it blames someone else for having done.
Mr. Speaker, we must first of all ask ourselves whether the present society is not as barbarous as it could be centuries ago. Even today, do we not see murders which are acknowledged even by the authorities of all countries in the world?
Mr. Speaker, there are still wars going on that are so cruel as to exceed the greatest cruelties of a few centuries ago.
I ask myself whether society as it is now deserves abolition of the death penalty. That is the very serious question which comes to my mind. Crime of every kind are more prevalent than ever within our society, Humanitarianism has not only failed to develop but has on the contrary declined. I therefore ask myself serious questions and say: Since society, because of its failure to become humanitarian, does not deserve the abolition of the death penalty, although it would be ideal, we should retain, in such a society, means which rationally would seem obsolete.
Thus, what should prompt us to settle the matter and take a stand? I think that in such a case, the people's opinion must be relied upon and expressed in the House.
Cases where capital punishment should be maintained should perhaps be determined in a more precise way. I agree with that. For example, I cannot see why a difference should be made between a prison guard or a policeman and an ordinary citizen. In fact, I believe that all citizens are equal, whatever their functions may be.
It could be argued that policemen or prison guards run more risks of being attacked and that it is why capital punishment is maintained in their case. However, a statistical survey would show that everybody is in danger. The high number of traffic accidents shows how dangerous it is just to be out in the street.
In spite of the respect I have for policemen and guards, I must say they chose their occupation of their own free
Capital Punishment
will. What is more, they have all they need to defend themselves and I fail to see why that distinction should be made.
To my mind, the law should be more explicit: it should state precisely what murders carry the death penalty. We would then perhaps manage to prevent them, or even eliminate them totally.
Heinous crimes are also committed, where the culprit himself asks to be done away with, as in the case of Leopold Dion. I believe the public view is right in these circumstances.
The two previous speakers said, and I am of the same opinion, that more attention should be paid the victim than the criminal.
To conclude, I would say that we should try capital punishment as we have tried its abolition. In fact, this punishment has been abolished for much more than five years, as it was the custom even before 1967 to commute death penalty to life imprisonment.
Consequently, capital punishment has not been imposed for several years. Why not give it a real try providing, and I repeat, we specify in which case murder would be punishable by death.
Mr. Speaker, this of course is a very serious question but there is no other way we can reason under these circumstances.
If at least alternatives were put forward in order that a criminal could pay his debt to society otherwise than through capital punishment, our thinking might be different. But there is absolutely nothing in this respect and one could ask therefore if it would not be better to put more into the studying of means which could eliminate crime; the problem of finding the appropriate punishment would then subside. As most people, I believe for instance that some offenders enjoy living at the expense of the state in our prisons and penitentiaries. The taxpayers see their dollars helping support offenders. I understand their resentment against such people and their wish to get rid of them at any cost. However if we found some means of putting those people to work and making them productive, the taxpayers could say: Well, those offenders have really paid their debt to society.
Therefore, I wonder if we could not revert to procedures providing the offenders an opportunity to pay their debt to society by becoming productive citizens and rendering some services to society. Since we have not yet reached that stage, I believe that now, in 1973, there is no solution but to retain imposition of the death penalty in very precise cases.

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this being the first time I have had an opportunity of rising to speak in this parliament, I would like to bring to you greetings and congratulations from the many wonderful people it is my pleasure to represent in the electoral district of Red Deer. I thank you for affording me this opportunity of speaking on their behalf in this debate.

January 29, 1973
Capital Punishment
Mr. Speaker, over the years the average Canadian citizen has put a great deal of thought into the ways and means of controlling those who perpetrate crime. Could we, just for a moment, take a look at what constitutes an average Canadian? A Canadian is not a violent individual in any sense of the word. He or she is not barbaric, nor could one say they could be construed as being revengeful but, rather, he or she is a kindly, God-fearing person. Mr. Speaker, if you look closely you will find him to be basically honest, straightforward, hard working, seeking the opportunity to love and to be loved. He will be found to be one who recognizes the rights of others and who in return expects others to recognize his rights as an individual in this big, overwhelming world.
You will find a Canadian to be a person who appreciates the privileges that have been afforded him as a citizen of this great land; a person crying out for everybody to inject into society a little bit of common sense and justice for the common good. You will find an individual who wants to be treated as a human being, not as a mere number among the masses. He wants, not only for this generation but for future generations, retention of the basic rights of freedom of speech, freedom of worship and freedom of living and travelling through this fair land without the fear of being molested or struck down. You will find an individual who believes in maintaining and enforcing law and order.
Mr. and Mrs. Average Canadian live by the law and expect others to do the same. Recognition is given to the many laws which guide thought and action and which have a definite effect on the well-being of all. Through their eyes, let us look for a moment as Canadians at the infinite law of nature as laid down by the Divine Creator. There are basically, to all intents and purposes, two kingdoms in this world-the plant kingdom and the animal kingdom. The photosynthesis and growth which takes place in the plant kingdom complements the respiration and growth of the animal kingdom. One is dependent on the other for maximum growth and development.
Mr. Speaker, this is the basic law of creation laid down for the benefit of man until man decides, as a result of his craving, to disrupt the process. Whatever his reasoning may be for breaking this law, somebody is going to pay the penalty. It could be a law of the environment which is broken, which will prove to be detrimental to somebody or something, regardless of whether it is an oil spill, excess smoke or the misuse of chemicals. Somebody will have to suffer.
Take the law of electricity as an example. Electricity has proven to be one of the greatest benefits to modern society as we know it today and is one of the main basic energy forces in the world created for mankind. Engineers know how to develop it; they know how to control it; they know how to use it. But can they see it? No, they cannot. If an individual comes into contact with this force, he breaks the law of electricity, and we all know that the result can be instant death.
Mr. Speaker, look for a moment if you will at the law of gravity, another part of the perfect law. We know that if the gravitational pull of the earth were too little, we would float off into space; if it became too great, we would not be able to move on the earth's surface. If a man breaks
this law by stepping off a cliff, for instance, we know what the end result would be.
I do not mention these facts of life to bore you, Mr. Speaker, but rather to remind this parliament that the people whom I represent, as do Canadians as a whole, respect these basic rules in the formation of man-made laws. Would it be too much to suggest that we, as elected representatives of this twenty-ninth parliament, are generally agreed on everything I have said to this point? But now comes the crunch. What do we do with those who break the rules in the game of life? What do we do with those who become so estranged and violent that they murder a fellow being deliberately, through passion, emotion, jealousy, hatred, greed or for any other reason? This is the question we have to deal with now.
As I mentioned earlier, Canadians are not a revengeful or barbaric people, as some suggest. I will not accept this as fact just because there are large numbers of people calling for capital punishment for those convicted of murder. When people call for capital punishment they are not necessarily calling for hanging. They are asking for the removal from society, in a humane manner, those who have proven beyond reasonable doubt that they cannot live under the code of life as laid down by the majority. Because of the concern of most Canadians and the divergence of opinion on this vital issue, I am convinced that the best way to reach an acceptable decision is to hold a national referendum in conjunction with the next federal election. As the minister is aware, I have a notice of motion on the order paper in this regard which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should introduce a measure to provide that, on polling day at the next federal election, there shall be held a national plebiscite on the question of the abolition of capital punishment and on the related and consequent questions arising therefrom.
In all seriousness I ask hon. members to accept this motion as a bill of the government to let the Canadian people become a part of true participatory democracy. Since the decision reached on this important issue will have a direct effect on the future well-being of society, I believe every Canadian should be allowed to make a personal choice in a matter of such magnitude.
In my opinion, the argument of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) against a national referendum is very weak. To say that to hold a plebiscite on capital punishment would open the way for other plebiscites is, in my opinion, utter nonsense. This would be the satisfactory and just way to settle this highly charged, emotional question. The minister has said that there will be a free vote. It makes me wonder if he has a fear of going to the people and letting them decide for themselves exactly what they want.
The growing concern of multitudes in this country is caused by the continuing increase of crime over the past five years. The day has gone when we can say, "It can't happen here." Mr. Speaker, anything that can happen anywhere in the world can happen in Canada. Some of the most dastardly murders that have been committed on this globe have been equalled here. Do I have to remind hon. members of the Laporte slaying and of the children

January 29, 1973

who are molested and either die or, if they survive, have their lives ruined?
Although it is not necessary to go into details here, the minister knows of many such instances, as we all do. He must realize that this increasing wave of crime is what people are crying against. No one feels safe any longer, and what hope is there for Canadians without a deterrent, an enforced deterrent? If the Solicitor General could prove to the people of this country that his department can bring crime under control, and also those who commit crimes, the Canadian people would not be so doubtful or uneasy. But I warn him now that they are not going to be thwarted much longer. There are thousands of Canadians who will not put their faith in or be guided by a government that seeks to abolish capital punishment and at the same time accepts a policy to legalize abortions. For many thousands of seriously thinking people these two proposals cannot be equated.
Canadians, as a whole, are a forgiving people and I would venture to say that by far the vast majority would lend a helping hand to anyone in trouble. Why, then, would those who contemplate crime take a club or a gun to break the law when such help is available? In my opinion, our people would not be so upset over this issue if they had any hope that justice would prevail and that crime would be controlled. Capital punishment is the only hope in controlling murder. Canadian citizens are holding on to this concept as hard as they can because since 1967 they have seen crimes occur which never should have been committed in a civilized country. Instead of the situation improving, unfortunately it is worsening.
I do not deny that Canadians have compassion for those who have broken the law, but I believe they have more compassion for those who are the victims of lawless action. I refer to parents, sisters and brothers of murdered children; I refer to the young mother and 22-month old baby who are left without a husband and father, murdered while on duty as a policeman just recently. Yes, Mr. Speaker, these are the real victims; these are the people whom Mr. and Mrs. Canadian are trying to protect when they press for capital punishment.
According to statistics, capital punishment is a deterrent. A report prepared by Statistics Canada for the Department of the Solicitor General reveals that an average of 222 persons, excluding police officers and prison guards, were murdered in each of the seven years before the partial ban came into effect. The annual average went up to 376 between 1968 and 1971, the last full year for which figures are available. The total for 1971 is 422 non-police murders. I quote for the benefit of the House a recent statement attributed to a law enforcement officer in Ottawa:
In conversing with criminals while being transported to Kingston, the reason many criminals gave for not carrying a revolver was to avoid the possibility of execution resulting from the death of a victim.
Another police officer has recently stated:
No worse time than the present could be chosen for the abolition of the death penalty. We must decide whether we are going to protect society against the criminal or protect the criminal against society.
Capital Punishment
Many Canadians believe this. I realize the minister has a great responsibility to protect those who have broken the law, but he has a much more serious responsibility to protect society. His duty is to lessen and control the ravages of crime which at the present time is growing and is out of control. What is being done to protect people from the increased use of drugs which has resulted in some murders? Never in history has there been a time as today. When the younger generation has been subjected to such lawlessness and all its influences.
If parliament removes this deterrent to crime without taking into consideration the individual wishes of people of this country, how, then, will we face those who are personally affected by unwarranted murder? Capital punishment cannot be a deterrent if it is not enforced, neither can life imprisonment be a deterrent if the sentence is not served.

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have an opportunity to speak in this debate on capital punishment, a subject, to be sure, that is very important from all points of view. I think those of us who have come to the House since 1966-1967, when the suspension of hanging was agreed to, will be concerned that we do not spend a great deal of time threshing old straw or debating ideas that have already been well discussed in this place. Nevertheless, as I say, this is a very important debate not only to those people who may become subject to the law we pass here but also as an indication of the direction our society is taking at this stage of its national development.
I believe there is much concern in the United States, as well as in this country, over the recent public mass murders and gangland slayings that have occurred, as well as over the regular diet on television during the past several years of war and murder. I believe there is real concern as to whether our country, indeed our whole generation, is suffering from the brutalizing effects of this particular diet on our television screen every night. Fortunately, the Viet Nam war is almost at an end, at least we hope it is, with the signing of the pact this past week end. But there can be little doubt that a whole generation of people in North America have been witnessing the kind of program I have referred to on television, which is why I say there is concern whether there has been any brutalizing effect therefrom.
It will be interesting to see, both in this debate and in the public debate that follows along with it, whether our Canadian society has moved toward a more human position than was the case five years ago and whether we in this generation really do abhor the thought of murder as much as did the previous generation.
I was interested, when the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) spoke, to hear him say he did not feel this debate was important enough to command our time in the House at this particular stage. It seems to me there can be no question but that this debate has to take place now. Surely the issue of capital punishment is inherently important in our society, not only to people who are charged with murder and other crimes but to the whole society. It is indeed difficult to imagine a question of greater social

January 29, 1973
Capital Punishment
significance than the grounds on which the state claims the right to deprive a citizen of his life. The legislation establishing, defining and circumscribing this right is surely important and involves one of the most fundamental decisions confronting any society at any time. It goes to the very core of our society's philosophy, reflecting and probably helping to create as well the values and norms which permeate all human social intercourse.
Secondly, it seems that this debate is important because of the kind of public opinion which has been generated during the past months and especially during the past weeks as a result of the number of newspaper articles, editorials and television programs we have had relating to the subject, as well as the number of letters Members of Parliament are receiving. It is our responsibility as representatives of the Canadian people to come to grips with this issue at this time.
Thirdly, Mr. Speaker, there is the question of our obligation to enact legislation to replace the previous five-year law which expired on December 29 last. To ignore this issue would be to shirk our responsibility as members of this House of Commons. In the field of criminal law and punishment, as in all others, we must establish policy by design, by responsible, thoughtful and wide deliberation, and not by default.
I recognize the complexity of the issue now before this House, the difficulty of interpreting the relevant statistical data and the sincerity with which honest and responsible men hold divergent views. I want to make my own position clear. In principle I am in favour of the abolition of the death penalty. I regard capital punishment as morally repugnant, ineffective as a deterrent and inadequate as a means of ensuring the protection of our society.
I believe that the convictions of many hon. members on this matter are based as such on subjective theory as on a detached appraisal of statistical evidence. Indeed, I would venture to suggest that most people who have adopted a position on this issue have done so as the result of a sort of inner feeling or reaction which is conditioned by their background, their experience and their philosophy. That renowned criminal lawyer, Clarence Darrow, was no doubt right when he observed half a century ago that "questions of this sort are not settled by reason; they are settled by prejudices and sentiments or by emotion."
Given my own predisposition and the grave implications of state-sanctioned execution, it would require a considerable body of uncontestable evidence proving the effectiveness of capital punishment as a deterrent to persuade me of the merits of the death penalty. Like other members of this House, I have read many reports, studies and analyses on the subject and I am not convinced that any significant link has been established between retention or abolition of the death penalty, on one hand, and the incidence of murder on the other. Indeed, the overwhelming weight of evidence, the opinions of professional psychologists, sociologists and criminologists leads to the conclusion that no such correlation exists. It seems to me that in nearly every country in the world the trend is to less and less capital punishment. Whether there actually is a law providing for capital punishment or not, there is a tendency to carry out fewer and fewer executions.
(Mr. Foster.]
If we consider France, where they still have capital punishment-incidentally, they still use the guillotine which was made famous during the French revolution- we find that between 1953 and 1969 only 22 out of 85 persons sentenced to capital punishment were actually guillotined. This country, which actually has a capital punishment law on the books, is moving toward fewer and fewer executions. Likewise, in the United States between 1965 and 1971 there were ten executions carried out, and those were all under state laws. There have been none under federal law in that country where they have criminal law both in the state and at the federal level.
I would venture to suggest that more statistics have been produced and cited on this subject than on any other. It is not my intention to bombard the House with statistics. Let me just say that there is no such study in which I have found evidence that demonstrates to my satisfaction the effectiveness of capital punishment as a deterrent.
In Europe, those countries which have abolished the death penalty have no higher murder rates; in fact, in many instances they have significantly lower rates than those which have retained the death penalty. In the United States, the abolitionist states have no higher murder rates; in fact, they tend to have lower rates than adjacent states which have retained capital punishment. In those states where the death penalty has been abolished there is no appreciable difference in homicide rates before and after abolition.
In our own country, the result of our recently expired five-year experimental period-though the evidence is still incomplete and tentative-tends to demonstrate yet again that capital punishment has no deterrent effect. The excellent study of Dr. Fattah is most persuasive on this point. Let me quote, in support of this argument, a United Nations' document on capital punishment, published in 1968. That document sums up the position in the following words:
With respect to the influence of the abolition of capital punishment upon the incidence of murder, all of the available data suggest that where the murder rate is increasing, abolition does not appear to hasten the increase; where the murder rate is decreasing, abolition does not appear to interrupt the decrease; where the rate is stable, the presence or absence of capital punishment does not appear to affect it.
It is interesting to note in passing that many authorities even argue that the death penalty, by contributing to a climate of violence and by appealing to the suicidal tendencies of some unbalanced people, actually tends to increase the incidence of murder.
Let me reiterate my own conclusion, Mr. Speaker. I can find no evidence of correlation in either direction between capital punishment and the incidence of murder in our society. To advocate the death penalty as a deterrent to murder seems to me to imply an underlying conception of human conduct and motivation to which I do not subscribe. It assumes a rationality of behaviour on the part of potential murderers, a deliberate choice between alternative courses of action based on calculated consequences and anticipated pleasure and pain. It is now generally acknowledged, however, that much of human behaviour is unplanned and habitual rather than calculated and deliberate.
January 29, 1973

Can we deny, Mr. Speaker, that in the case of homicide this aspect of human behaviour is particularly apparent? Very few murders result from cold, calculated plotting. The overwhelming proportion are crimes of passion, committed in the heat of the moment, often resulting from domestic quarrels and frequently associated with drink or drugs. Such crimes are every bit as deplorable and grievous as those committed with deliberate intent but-and this is the point I want to make-they involve no premeditation and no calculation of consequences. In these cases, and in the cases involving mentally deranged killers, the deterrent value of capital punishment, or indeed of any other penalty, is irrelevant. In short, Mr. Speaker, deterrence, if it has any significance at all, can only operate upon rational minds; and people in a rational frame of mind do not commit murders. This is the central dilemma, as I see it, of the "deterrent" school of thought.
In looking back over history, the trend toward a more humane treatment of criminals is unmistakable. It is shocking and frightening to be reminded that only a century and a half ago-as late as the early 1800s-teenage boys and girls were hanged for petty theft and for picking pockets. When offences such as these were removed from the list of crimes punishable by death, great cries arose, sincere no doubt, to express profound fears for the safety of persons and property. It is frightening to realize, too, that it was only a few centuries ago that men were burned at the stake, boiled in oil, broken on the wheel and subjected to the most hideous kinds of brutal torture, all in the name of justice and for the sake of deterrence. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether future generations will look back on our present debate with the same feelings that we now experience in regard to these earlier punishments.
In this historical evolution of criminal punishment, the total and permanent abolition of capital punishment marks a logical, perhaps inevitable step. We have come some distance in creating a more humane approach to the treatment of criminals. I cannot help but think that we in Canada are now in the throes of the last, long, agonizing step in this process of evolution.
Many countries, indeed, have already overcome this last hurdle. Many other countries have officially abolished or unofficially suspened the death penalty. Today, there are some 50 countries in the world where some form of capital punishment for certain crimes still exists. It is perhaps noteworthy that almost half of all executions in the noncommunist world take place in South Africa, which has an average of one execution, usually of a black, every three days. Britain, after a five-year trial period, permanently abolished the death penalty in 1970. The United States supreme court has recently declared the death penalty under most circumstances unconstitutional.
Most statisticians acknowledge that five years is an insufficient period of time to permit a conclusive determination of the trend in the murder rate. I believe that the last two years of statistics for the five-year trial period are not yet available. To be frank, I doubt that any further evidence will be adduced that will cause convinced abolitionists or retentionists to alter their positions. I do think, however, that many people are as yet undecided on the
Capital Punishment
merits of the case. For them, another trial period will provide an opportunity to gain additional information on which to base their judgment.
However one interprets the present evidence of public feeling on the issue of capital punishment, it is unmistakably clear that serious divisions of view exist within our country. A matter of this importance, I believe, should have as much public consensus as possible. Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) is to the effect that for certain types of convicted murderers there should be a mandatory 25 years' sentence before the normal parole procedure will be considered. This would not only apply to convicted murderers of police officers and prison guards but also to certain type of murders which occur at the time of other violent crimes. When this amendment is moved at the committee stage, I think it should be given very serious consideration. The public of this country is concerned that there is not adequate protection from this type of criminal. It seems to me that the mobster or the hired killer is the type of person from whom people are demanding protection. Perhaps this type of criminal should be incarcerated for this long period before parole is considered.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me emphasize that I am concerned with he protection of society and with the adequacy of our present rehabilitation system. We should re-examine the ways in which we administer our penitentiary policies, our parole system and our leave of absence programs. Certainly we should continue our pursuit of the basic causes of crime, its nature, its prevention and its detection. In this way we can combine an effective and humane treatment of offenders with the maximum degree of public safety. I am confident that we are on the right road. Let us not now turn back.

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by the time we finish this debate we will have canvassed all the historical, philosophical, statistical, moral and religious aspects of this issue. Let me preface my remarks by saying that thus far there appears to be a trend with regard to a vote which will be uncomfortably close and therefore it is necessary to present the varying views to persuade members of the House of the importance of this issue.
I think the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) set the tone of the debate and presented arguments in favour of the bill in a quiet, persuasive and telling way. I happen to be a total abolitionist but I am prepared to accept Bill C-2 and extend the law a further five years on the same basis as it was in 1967, because of the necessity of gaining further public support and because of the minister's statement that we are on the road to abolition.
This important social issue embraces all the emotional, mental and spiritual values of members of this House and therefore it will help to reflect that no one possesses all truth and all virtue and that only light can chase away the darkness. That is why I respect the thought and feelings of every person who holds views contrary to mine. But I am quick to add that my view is not a bleeding-heart plea for abolition; my motive is for a more human and decent society rather than misplaced pity for the offender. I am

January 29, 1973
Capital Punishment
deeply encouraged and strengthened by the report, publicly stated, of leaders in the community-church leaders, social workers, penologists, parole workers, and so on, who have expressed their concern, their conviction, their commitment and have indicated the worth of the individual and the redemptive powers of their teaching and their experience.
Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General has said that we are on the road to abolition. This is because of recent changes in the law and the exercise of commutation which have resulted not only in de jure abolition but also in de facto abolition. Not since 1962 has a person been hanged in Canada. Canada has joined other countries in a gradual movement away from capital punishment and is concentrating on alternative methods of effective control. The amendments of 1961 introduced by a Conservative government, by the Hon. Davie Fulton, brought a sharp change in the attitude toward capital punishment. The bill which made a division of murder into capital and noncapital, with the automatic right of appeal even to the Supreme Court of Canada, the polling of the jury as to a recommendation of mercy which was to be forwarded to the Minister of Justice, and the abolition of the death penalty for persons under 18 years, plus the almost full exercise of the royal prerogative of mercy set the change in motion.
The Progressive Conservative party under the leadership of the Hon. Davie Fulton set the change in motion. The debate on that bill in 1966, and the passing of the new bill in 1967 which was introduced by the Liberal government, placed a heavy emphasis on abolition and stressed a move away from capital punishment. Both parties, the Progressive Conservative party and the Liberal party, are to be commended on this move to de facto abolition. Dr. C. H. S. Jayewardine summarizes his view of the movement to de facto abolition in the following way:
Both parties sought to produce the change by executive rather than legislative action. Both parties were goaded into moving the bills that they finally introduced. That the one is now viewed as a retentionist and the other as abolitionist does not appear to be because of their ideological commitment but because of the result of the circumstances in which they were situated. It was the Liberal government's legislation that limited the imposition of the penalty of deith to almost the point of abolition but then the legislation which the Conservative government had been earlier forced to introduce left the Liberal government no choice in the further legislation that they were then forced to introduce. It was the Liberal government that commuted every sentence of death but then the pattern of commutation set by previous Conservative governments left them no choice. It was as if destiny was unfolding itself unobtrusively so as to make the change that was occurring appear congruous with the will of the people.
I would ask the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) to note that change in attitude of the Progressive Conservative party and the Liberal party when considering the move toward de facto abolition. This move, Mr. Speaker, is no different than it has been in other countries throughout the world. When I think that in the year 1840 the small country of Luxemburg moved to abolish capital punishment, and here in 1973-150 years later-the country of Canada is now moving in the same direction, it makes me realize that maybe we are moving not too quickly in comparison with other countries.

England has moved. She commenced her move in 1965 and almost completed abolition in 1969. In 1972 we had the supreme court of the United States bring down an historic and dramatic judgment in which it said that capital punishment constituted cruel and unusual punishment and therefore violated sections 8 and 14 of the United States Constitution. This now is an attempt by Canada to march with the times.
Why am I an abolitionist? There are four main reasons. First, I believe in the basic worth and value of human life. Albert Schwietzer said it beautifully in the words "reverence for life" in the twenty-first century, and Jesus and Gandhi propounded the philosophy and lived it. In the debate on the bill in 1967 the former solicitor general said:
I believe that so long as the state claims the right under the law to deliberately take human life there will be a tendency to regard life more cheaply.
I believe that reverence for life is substantially diminished when we base our law on revenge and retribution, and that reverence for life is substantially increased when we base our law on redemption, reformation and rehabilitation. My second reason for being an abolitionist is that many innocent people have been hanged in the past and many innocent people may be hanged in the future. Judicial courts, even with all the safeguards of appeal procedures, are not infallible. False testimony, mistaken identification, biased juries or misinterpreted circumstantial evidence all make it possible that an innocent person may hang. This is the reason for Lafayette's challenge, "I shall ask for abolition of the death penalty until I have the infallibility of human judgment demonstrated to me." This is why it goes unanswered by the retentionists.
Mr. Speaker, you will recall the debate in 1967 and the mention of the Christie case in England, which at that time indicated the wrong person had been executed and that this evidence did not come out until the execution had taken place. We remember the D'Arcy McGee murder in Canada which left many doubts as to whether the correct person was executed. And many of us have had agonizing question marks with regard to the guilt of the young man Truscott. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we feel that the death penalty is so final, so irreversible that it almost prompts the statement: I would rather see one hundred guilty men go free than one innocent man executed. This is why there is such a low conviction rate in Canada and elsewhere throughout the world; it is because of the reluctance of judges and juries to bring in a conviction because of the possibility of mistake. Therefore they grapple for and grasp at alternative verdicts.
The third reason I am an abolitionist is that people do not have equal opportunities before the courts. The scales are weighted against the poor and inarticulate. We cannot consider this problem of capital punishment and we cannot consider the act of murder without bringing into consideration the social, the economic, the cultural and the racial factors that are brought into play. Lewis E. Hawes, a former warden of Sing Sing penitentiary in the United States, has written, "Those who are executed are always poor and friendless." He has indicated that money assures the best counsel and the highest chance of acquittal.
January 29, 1973

Differences in racial, cultural and social status discriminate against the poor and the friendless. There is an old Indian saying, "Judge not a man until you have stood in his moccasins." How can we judge the man who has committed murder? How would you like to stand in the shoes of a negro in the southern states, charged with murder for rape, when he has full knowledge that never has a white person in the southern states been convicted of a similar offence?
How would you like to stand in the shoes of a young Canadian Indian when all the cards are stacked against you on economic, social and racial grounds? I hasten to add that we have gone a long way in changing the law and providing all with equal opportunities before the courts. Legal aid and the provision of lawyers in capital murder cases are steps in the right direction, but they do not meet all the inequities that still prevail under the law.
Fourthly, society is largely responsible for the conditions which breed crime and we must accept part of the blame. Violence has been rampant in the world these last few years, and violence begets violence. Just think of half a million men returning from Viet Nam. They have been trained and have experience in killing and they will come back and try to adjust to the American way of life. That will be difficult, Mr. Speaker. I do not doubt that many will encounter difficulties and will commit crimes which call for capital punishment.
The use of guns in society is another problem we must face. Here I recall the fate of the bill which Senator Kennedy brought before the American Congress. Its purpose was to prohibit the use of certain guns in the United States. Hon. members will recall the difficulties that he encountered. He met with no success in securing passage of that bill; it would not pass in Congress. Let me add quickly that an amendment to the Explosives Act was brought forward in the previous parliament. Differences and divergencies of opinion on restrictions affecting the use of guns and the use of ammunition sharply divided the members of this House. We did not come to any final conclusion on the bill.
I have said that society breeds crime. Poor economic conditions, poor employment prospects and lack of decent housing create a kind of desperation, a kind of alienation which form the bedrock in the breeding of crime. One might ask, what is required? Without doubt, we must emphasize the need for improving basic conditions to do with housing, to do with prison programs and to do with the acceptance of responsibilities on the part of inmates so as to bring about their employment and integration into the community. Please notice that I speak of integration into the community, not reintegration. Many men who have spent time in penitentiaries have never been integrated as part of the community; therefore, we cannot talk in terms of reintegration but must talk of integration.
At this stage I wish to commend the former solicitor general who had the courage and wisdom to bring forward changes in our penal system and in the treatment of prisoners. That action took courage and it brought on him criticism not only from members of the House but from many people across Canada. I think time will show that
Capital Punishment
the former solicitor general was on the right track in developing such programs.
The age most critical for young people, the age at which they are most apt to get into trouble, is that between 16 and 24. That is why we in the NDP were deeply concerned over the young offenders bill brought forward in the last parliament. Evidence given before the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs by social workers and other public officials indicated the need for diagnostic and related services to be used in cases involving young people. I for one am happy that I attempted to block passage of that bill. If we are ever to solve this problem and create the type of society in which young people will be less likely to commit murder, we must seek the support of our youth. We must introduce diagnostic and related services that will help us to meet some of the problems that youth encounters today.
We have heard many arguments against abolition and will continue hearing them. It is safe to say that deterrence and the protection of society are the main arguments put forward. Mr. Speaker, I cannot stand statistics, having found that they can be brought forward to support whichever side is preferred. Statistics fail to disclose the facts because they fail to take into account factors involving social, economic, cultural, educational and racial problems which play a far more important part in deterring crime than punishment.
United Nations' reports indicate that the examination of records of the number of murders committed before and after the abolition or reintroduction of the death penalty do not support the theory that capital punishment has a unique deterrent effect. It has been said, and will be repeated again, that if capital punishment is carried to its logical conclusion, then if we are to emphasize the deterrent aspect there ought to be public hangings across Canada. Let us set up a scaffold on the grounds of Parliament Hill, perhaps we should set up a scaffold in the civic square outside the city hall, perhaps we should set up a scaffold on the Expo property in Montreal and publicly display a scaffold in Stanley Park, Vancouver.

speechtext: A good idea.

speechtext:
This will bring such revulsion when people see what happens to a person who is hanged that capital punishment would come to an immediate end. Studies have indicated that in England during the nineteenth century, of 167 pickpockets who were hanged 164 had seen others hanged publicly. Actually, many of them plied their trade when witnessing the hanging of other pickpockets.
Professor Selling attempted to test the argument that capital punishment offers special protection to police officers by comparing police homicides in abolitionist and retentionist states. While stressing the special difficulties of such a test, Professor Selling reports that "on the whole the abolitionist states . . . seem to have fewer (police) killings but the differences are small".
I would be remiss in my duty if I did not point out that recent public opinion polls indicate that there is a sharp trend in favour of retention. Public acceptance of retention is a relevant but not controlling factor. We must remember that society does not practise what it preaches.

January 29, 1973
Capital Punishment
The steady decrease in executions across the world persuasively demonstrates that capital punishment is unacceptable to society today. One member who spoke earlier this evening mentioned a referendum and suggested that a referendum on the subject ought to be held at the next election. That course, Mr. Speaker, would be a dereliction of the duty of a Member of Parliament.

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
We are sent here to represent the constituents of our ridings and are expected to inform ourselves on the issues. We are expected to exercise common sense in our judgments. Sending the issue of capital punishment back to the voters in the form of a referendum would be a complete dereliction of our duty. It would not be necessary for us to be here, for all issues could be decided by referendum. Can you imagine what would happen if the imposition of taxes' was determined on the basis of referendum?
Our best protection would be the introduction of basic reforms in the treatment and confinement of inmates. These are needed. It is also necessary to differentiate between different types of murder. Two out of every three murders are crimes of passion committed within the family circle. There is very little likelihood of repetition. The difficult issue is detecting the psychotic and containing him until he is fully restored. This would require research programs, treatment and reformation. This is why we say the Parole Act should be studied in detail so as to find out ways and means of detecting the psychotic killer and devising the programs and research necessary to deal with him.
I direct my final remarks to the new members in this chamber. After sitting here for a good number of years they will ask themselves, "What have I done to make this a better Canada?" And they might find difficulty in deciding. I might as well be personal, I have been here for seven years and I find it very difficult to answer that question. The role of the opposition is that of constructive criticism. This having been said, I feel proud of my own contribution to the final form of the young offenders bill and take pleasure in that achievement. The former hon. member for Welland, Mr. Donald Tolmie, made a significant contribution to the formation of the law permitting the expunging of criminal records. For his part in this legislation he is to be congratulated. Many of us have enjoyed the same kind of satisfaction that he did.
I would say to the new members, "If you want an opportunity to do something which will put Canada in a forward position, which will underline the compassion which is to be found in most of us, you have an opportunity to vote in support of the bill now before this chamber." If we concentrate on the changes which are taking place in terms of treatment, rather than revert to revenge and retribution, we shall march forward and we shall be able to say as the years go by that we have done a good job.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in this debate to explain that at the third reading stage, I shall vote against this bill in keeping with the position I

took in this House in 1967. I will explain my situation by repeating some of the arguments put forward by the Solicitor General (M. Allmand) who stated, as recorded on page 688 of Hansard for January 26, 1973, and I quote:
The purpose of the original trial period in 1967 was to allow for a period during which those crimes punishable by death would be severely restricted. This five-year experiment would be a time of intense study and analysis, the results of which were to guide the House's deliberations after December 29, 1972. We are beyond the termination date of that five-year period but, unfortunately, we do not have the full data for the entire five years on which to base studies and, hence, legislative recommendations.
And further on:
It seems to me that we must see the process, commenced in 1967, through to its logical conclusion.
I want to be true to my convictions of 1967 even though, of course, I respect the contrary opinions of my colleagues. I hope they will consider mine favourably. In 1967, I voted against the bill when a free vote was held, regardless of the party line. In 1973, it will also be a free vote. In view of the fact that I have not heard further arguments against my former position, I think I must explain to the House why I will vote in the same manner as in 1967.
I am told that I have not changed. I did not change precisely because the arguments put forward by the Solicitor General himself and by the other members who until now have participated in the debate have not convinced me. I think I am entitled to my opinion in spite of what some members who say I have not changed may think.
Mr. Speaker, I note that the Canadian people are taking a tougher stand with regard to certain acts committed since 1967 and which were witnessed in Quebec and in other provinces. I note that the people are becoming more and more strict and are increasingly asking the government to pass a legislation designed to protect them against a seemingly greater degree of violence than when we enacted a similar legislation in 1967.
The act which abolished capital punishment for a certain type of murder expired on December 29, 1972.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I will probably repeat some arguments which were put forward in this House, but I believe that in such an important debate, it is difficult to avoid repetitions. We heard many repetitions in 1964 during the debate on the national flag when some 200 speeches were delivered, and I think that many arguments were then repeated. Nevertheless, each member is entitled to express his views on the bill now under consideration.
I said that except in the case of police officers or prison guards, capital murder was no longer involved.
The bill now under consideration would actually reinstate those provisions, but would substitute to the terms capital murder and non-capital murder the terms murder that is punishable by death and murder that is punishable by life imprisonment.
If the bill were passed, the provisions which have been in force during the past five years would remain for five more years, i.e. until December 31, 1977.
January 29, 1973

In case the amendments were not renewed or permanently adopted before December 31, 1977, we would again come under the act which was in force prior to 1967.
Clauses 8 and 9 of the bill provide for interim measures which will become necessary in case these provisions are adopted in the near future. Those interim measures are all the more necessary because, theoretically, since December 29 1972, the pre-1967 provisions have been restored.
If the bill before us were passed, it would not be fair for people not to benefit by its provisions merely because they fell under the act between December 29, 1972 and the coming into force of this bill, since normally it should have been introduced in the House before expiry of the five-year period, i.e. before December 29, 1972, in order to come immediately into effect on December 30.
I believe, therefore, that on second reading I shall not object to the bill being referred to the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for detailed study; but the House will again have to deal with the bill and, unless amendments are proposed which coincide with the position I took early in my statement, I shall have to vote against it on third reading, as I did in 1967. On the other hand, I know that some hon. members intend to propose amendments, although I do not know exactly what they are. If some of those strike me as judicious, I shall be happy to support them; but if the bill rejects the death penalty, I shall have to vote against it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is an old story that has gone the rounds in many countries and, if I can paraphrase it, it is the story of a man who was sleeping and dreamed he was speaking in the House of Commons on the subject of capital punishment. And when he awoke, by golly, he was! You and me, Mr. Speaker, have both had the opportunity now on two separate occasions to listen to a debate in this chamber encompassing this important subject, and as I was sitting here this evening I was thinking how valuable it was to have the requirement in our rules that a matter cannot be debated twice in one session. However, it now seems that we have not taken enough precautions to have some extensive requirement to prevent this House of Commons from coming back regularly to debate certain issues that seem destined to be debated on into eternity. As has already been mentioned on a number of occasions in this debate, this matter was very exhaustively dealt with by parliament in 1966 and 1967; now in 1973 it is being debated again.
Indeed, this debate has a kind of Mackenzie King quality to it; the debate is so unreal. We are, in effect, asked to extend provisions that would partially abolish that which has already been abolished, as has been noted by previous speakers, for the better part of the last decade. Indeed, I think it is assumed in all parts of the House and by all hon. members that, regardless of the outcome of the debate, the practice that has become very firmly entrenched and accepted in this country today of abolishing capital punishment will be continued.
Perhaps I have missed it, but I have not heard it seriously suggested either inside or outside the House that this
Capital Punishment
practice, which has been carried on extensively now by a number of successive governments, would be or should be discontinued. It therefore must strike many observers as passing strange that we should be launched once again, not on a debate of the kind we had in 1966 to abolish capital punishment but on a debate to almost abolish capital punishment, which I assume has really the end effect merely of satisfying some people more than others. Perhaps before too long there should be an opportunity to have some clear settlement of this issue if only to relieve parliament, let alone the general public, of this continued preoccupation with capital punishment.
As previous speakers have suggested, we are in very great danger, I think particularly in present circumstances when we are perpetuating this debate, of avoiding some of the fundamental issues that concern many hundreds of thousands of Canadians. We are going through a very serious time of economic and social dislocation in this country. We hear about it daily. We read about it in our newspapers. We watch it on the television screen. We know the extent of the misery that many of our fellow Canadians share. Yet here we are involving ourselves in this kind of rarefied debate of a matter which, thank God, touches on the lives of very few Canadians. I suggest something is quite obviously wrong with the priorities of a government that insists on having a prolonged debate on a subject of this nature.
