subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-VIET NAM-PROPOSED PEACEKEEPING FORCE-SOURCE OF FUNDS TO COVER COST OF CANADIAN PARTICIPATION
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-VIET NAM-PROPOSED PEACEKEEPING FORCE-SOURCE OF FUNDS TO COVER COST OF CANADIAN PARTICIPATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, however brief it may be, as I rise for the first time in this parliament I should convey my congratulations to yourself and to my distinguished friend and colleague, the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave), on the elevation to his high post.
On January 16, in the midst of a flurry of questions in respect of the present situation in which Canada finds itself in Viet Nam, I rose and asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) whether he could in a general way at that point in time indicate to the House just who was going to pay for this very unreal excursion into peacekeeping in Viet Nam. The minister, quite properly, I suppose, with the range of knowledge available to him at the time, said he did not know, it was too early to tell and to the best of his knowledge at that time the only cost incurred would be the cost of salaries.
Things have changed quite a bit in the past few days since that question was posed. We do now have troops in Viet Nam, we do in fact have a multimillion dollar destroyer escort en route to water contiguous to Vietnamese waters, we have a Hercules apparently already standing by on the ground, and probably in their wisdom the government has seen fit to keep one or two 707s standing by in the event we have to get out. It would be a pleasure to pursue the reason for all this concern but I think we will have an opportunity to do that if we have a debate later this week.
What I am concerned about is just where the money is to come from. Our distinguished ambassador to France said on June 2, 1969, and I quote from page 9306 of Hansard for that date the last sentence in the second paragraph of the right-hand column:
We believe we can achieve the transition, barring unexpected international developments, within a defence budget which will be maintained for the next three years at its current dollar level.
This is what brought me to my feet the other day in the House and what brings me to my feet again tonight. I want to know where the money is to come from. This will involve more than just the cost of salaries. Will the defence budget, for example, be unfrozen in order to satisfy pay allowances? If it is not to be unfrozen, will attrition or further cutbacks in the armed forces budget provide that money for sustaining a peacekeeping operation of this nature and magnitude in Viet Nam?
Will manpower and capital programs suffer, and will there be further base consolidation? More forced attrition would, in my view-and I hope the view of all members of the House-be intolerable and the effects of it disastrous to morale and training programs. There is not enough money to do nearly the things that our Canadian armed forces have been assigned to do by this government.
I ask the distinguished parliamentary secretary where the money is to come from to pay the 2 per cent of the commission's costs in Viet Nam, and does he have any idea what those costs will be? These are questions to which I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) should properly have addressed himself in his initial indication to the House of what in fact we might be doing in connection with this observer role.
I doubt very much that the parliamentary secretary has a detailed response for me tonight, given his limited time, but I am interested in what the per diem cost will be, even if it is based on past experience. This 60-day business is for the birds. We have ships, planes and men over there, and the more people we put in Viet Nam, the more difficult it will be for us to get them out. We have been involved in similar operations in India, Pakistan, Palestine and Kashmir. We have been in Lebanon, West Iran, and we have been with the United Nations' Yemen observer commission. We have taken part in United Nations' emergency forces in Cyprus, and we have been involved in UN operations in the Congo, Korea and with the ICC. And now we are in Viet Nam.
These things are not done without a tremendous burden being placed on departmental budgets. The difference is, Mr. Speaker, that this time we are being asked to do something in the context of a frozen budget and in the absence of an indication from the Minister of National Defence of what the government's intentions are with respect to funding this operation and, indeed, the entire defence budget for the ensuing year. The three-year period called for by the former minister, Mr. Cadieux, has virtually expired. I hope that tonight the distinguished parliamentary secretary can give us some indication of how much this is going to cost and where the money is coming from. If it is going to come out of the defence budget, can he give us any indication of the government's intention and willingness to unfreeze once and for all the current defence budget?

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY-INQUIRY AS TO INCREASE IN BASIC AMOUNT AND LOWERING OF AGE OF ELIGIBILITY
OLD AGE SECURITY-INQUIRY AS TO INCREASE IN BASIC AMOUNT AND LOWERING OF AGE OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I should like to commend my hon. friend, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), for his attendance here tonight when a "late show" question is being put to him. This is a practice which I hope he will continue and it is a practice on his part that I would commend to other ministers.
On Monday, January 8, as recorded in Hansard at page 38, I put this question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare:
In view of the general reference in the throne speech to the taking of steps to improve the economic conditions of old age pensioners, may I ask the minister if those steps will include an increase in the basic amount of the old age security pension? Will they also include a lowering of the eligibility age?
The reply of the minister was in these words:
Mr. Speaker, I expect to be able to make a statement in the House on this subject later on.
The minister kept that promise by making a speech in the debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne on Thursday, January 11, and included in that speech was this sentence as found on page 202 of Hansard:
However I can assure hon. members that a substantial old age
Adjournment Debate
pension increase will be announced soon, and I hasten to add that it will not be a mere token increase.
Further on in that same paragraph he indicated a concern not only for those over age 65 but also for those under that age. The next day, Friday, January 12, in the speech that I made in the same debate I warmly welcomed the statement of the minister which I have just quoted and gave him my commendation on the attention he seemed to be paying to the department of which he is now the minister.
I may add that since that date there have been a number of other questions put to the minister. Maybe I am an optimistic type, but it seems to me that his answers have all been in the right direction. It does seem clear that something is going to be done to implement the promise in the Speech from the Throne and the promise made by the minister in his speech of January 11. If therefore, Mr. Speaker, I seem pleased with what the minister has said, and if I am optimistic and hopeful, why do I take the time of the House, even in a "late show" period, to press my question? Well, I suppose one learns from long experience in this place that even when things are promised, if one does not rise and press and demand them they don't come.
So I rise tonight to express to the minister the very strong hope that he is not going to be one of those ministers who take forever to implement the Liberal promises of 1919, but that he will act quickly. I remind him that what we are seeking, particularly those of us in this part of the House, is precisely what he has proposed-a substantial increase in the old age pension, not a mere token increase. I remind him also that we want that increase to be an increase in the basic rate of the old age pension. We want it added to the part of the pension that is paid universally, and without any means or income test.
I also remind the minister that we want him in some way to break the 65 age floor either to start paying pensions to all those between 60 and 65 who are out of the labour market or to start paying pensions to spouses of persons who are in receipt of the pension. In a nutshell, Mr. Speaker, these are the points that we hope will be part of an announcement soon, and of legislation which I trust will be introduced almost immediately after the announcement.
I am aware of conversations that the minister intends to hold with his provincial counterparts on Friday of this week, but he has told us that these are only a conversation, that those ministers do not have the power of veto over what he intends to do. Therefore, if it is too much to ask the minister to tell us tonight how much the increase is going to be and what he is going to do about the eligible age, I hope that at least he will confirm his promise that there is going to be action, that he will tell us tonight when the announcement is going to be made and when the legislation is going to be introduced. Mr. Speaker, I hope those dates are next week.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-AMENDMENT OF STATUTES AFFECTING EMPLOYMENT-LEGISLATIVE PRIORITY
PUBLIC SERVICE-AMENDMENT OF STATUTES AFFECTING EMPLOYMENT-LEGISLATIVE PRIORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 16 I asked a question of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) with respect to the amendment of statutes affecting the employment of public servants and the legislative priority of those amendments, as reported at p^age 331 of Hansard. The question arose as a result of representations made to me by public servants who expressed concern over the fact that the public service staff association had in 1971 made extensive representations to the legislative review committee chaired by John G. Dryden, wherein there were many suggestions made with respect to changes in public service legislation. That occurred in 1971.
In the intervening period many questions have been placed on the order paper and many questions asked in this House as to when there might be some report on the matter and some legislative enactment. At last in the Speech from the Throne at the beginning of the present session, there was brief reference to the amending of those two statutes which affect the working conditions of public servants. The questions having been asked, the minister replied:
I cannot do more than give assurance that amendments will be introduced this session. I will discuss the precise timing with the House leader.
A similar answer was given to the supplementary asked at that time. In view of the delays, and in view of the great number of public servants in the national capital area and other areas who are anxious to know the answer to this question, it is important to raise it. They want to know, for instance, the limits on arbitration, the limits on negotiation, the resolution of the problem respecting redundant employees, the classification of employees and the standards, norms and rules that would apply; who will be prohibited from collective bargaining and who will not be. Then there is the whole question of managerial employees and confidentiality of certain procedures. There is also the matter of appropriate procedures with respect to the settlement of arbitrations and disputes.
The question of the appropriate procedure with respect to settlement of arbitration, the concepts of retraining because of the introduction of new technology, the whole question of delegation of authority, all of these are important and a large segment of the public service has been waiting a long time for answers. I expressed to the Clerk of the House my feeling that I was not satisfied with the answer given and that there ought to be a statement made by the minister telling us when these matters would be brought forward.
In addition to the budget surplus generally, there is the whole question of the House of Commons staff, the Senate staff, the Governor General's staff, staff locally engaged abroad and all other staffs which have to deal with an employer but which, unfortunately, cannot deal with him on a proper basis with duly qualified representation. I ask the parliamentary secretary whether he is able at this time to give a precise answer. I hope he will tell me that he has consulted the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) who in turn has consulted the government House leader, and that he comes into the chamber prepared to give a precise answer to questions which so many public servants are asking.
It seems to me the federal government should be the leader and point the way to industry and other governments as to what is the proper relationship and balance. This question was asked so that the matter could be brought forward at the earliest possible date. I would appreciate hearing from the parliamentary secretary, and look forward, as do so many public servants, to hearing that after the unemployment insurance legislation public service matters are next on the list to be dealt with.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-AMENDMENT OF STATUTES AFFECTING EMPLOYMENT-LEGISLATIVE PRIORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret to tell the hon. member I am unable to give him the exact assurances he is seeking. There are a number of reasons for this. He is quite correct in assuming that the government does intend to introduce proposals relating to the Public Service Staff Relations Act and to the Public Service Employment Act during the present session. I am informed by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) that the House will be given ample opportunity to discuss these matters.
Unfortunately, I cannot give the House the precise dates on which these amendments will be introduced. There is a heavy legislative program in preparation and items such as the budget and resolutions flowing therefrom will have
